item.description: The Yokote-Masuda Manga Museum is Japan’s first museum dedicated to manga — it preserves and displays thousands of original hand-drawn manga pages (genga) by leading artists, in a climate-controlled archive that safeguards this fragile art form. Free general admission and rotating exhibitions make it a must for manga fans venturing into Akita. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Masuda, Yokote, Akita Hours ~10:00–18:00 (closed some days) Admission Free (general); special exhibits vary Time needed 1–1.

item.title: Zao Okama Crater Lake: Yamagata's Emerald Volcano — Guide
item.description: Zao’s Okama crater lake is one of Japan’s most spectacular volcanic phenomena — an almost perfectly circular caldera filled with water of an otherworldly emerald-green colour caused by dissolved sulphur compounds. The Zao Echo Line toll road reaches the rim, making this one of Japan’s most accessible volcanic craters, with the colour shifting between deep teal and bright lime with the weather. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Zao, Yamagata (Miyagi border) Hours Echo Line ~Apr–Nov, daytime Admission Toll road fee applies Time needed About 1 hour Best time Summer–autumn; clear days for best colour What to See The near-perfectly circular emerald-green crater lake.

item.title: Akahada Ware Pottery: Nara Craft Experience Guide
item.description: Akahada ware (Akahada-yaki) is one of Nara’s historic pottery styles, traditionally made around the Koriyama area with a warm, earthy character and often charming deer or Nara motifs. Hands-on workshops let you shape your own piece on the wheel or by hand, guided by a resident potter. 🗓️ At a Glance Where Nara/Koriyama kilns & studios Activity Wheel or hand-building pottery Price ~¥3,000–5,000 (plus firing/shipping) Duration 60–120 min Best for Craft lovers; a keepsake souvenir What to Know Akahada-yaki is a historic Nara ceramic, often with deer or Nara motifs.

item.title: Asuka & Ishibutai Kofun: Cradle of Japan — Nara Guide
item.description: Asuka is the rural cradle of the early Japanese state, a landscape of rice fields dotted with 6th–7th-century burial mounds, mysterious carved stones and ancient temple sites. Its centerpiece is the Ishibutai Kofun, Japan’s largest megalithic stone chamber — best explored slowly by rental bicycle. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Asuka village, Nara Pref. Hours Sites daytime; Ishibutai ¥300, ~8:30–17:00 Admission Free village; small site fees Time needed Half day Best time Spring & autumn; cycling weather What to See The Ishibutai Kofun, a giant exposed megalithic burial chamber.

item.title: Asuka-nabe: Nara's Milk Hot Pot — Food Guide
item.description: Asuka-nabe is a warming country hot pot from the ancient-capital region of Asuka: chicken and vegetables simmered in a creamy milk-and-dashi broth. Said to trace back to the Asuka era, when dairy first reached Japan, it’s a comforting, slightly surprising local specialty best enjoyed in winter. 🗓️ At a Glance Where Asuka village & Nara restaurants Dish Chicken & vegetables in milk-dashi broth Price ~¥1,500–3,000 Season Best in winter Best for A warming sit-down meal What to Know A creamy milk-and-dashi broth with chicken and seasonal vegetables.

item.title: Gango-ji Temple: Ancient Roof Tiles in Naramachi — Nara Guide
item.description: Gango-ji sits in the heart of Naramachi and is one of Japan’s oldest temples, tracing to Asuka-dera of the late 6th century. A UNESCO World Heritage site, its Gokurakubo hall still carries roof tiles laid over 1,400 years ago — the oldest in Japan. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Chuin-cho, Naramachi, Nara Hours 9:00–17:00 Admission ¥500 Time needed 30–45 min Best time Combine with a Naramachi stroll What to See The Gokurakubo hall, a National Treasure, with Japan’s oldest surviving roof tiles.

item.title: Hase-dera Temple: Peonies & Covered Stairway — Nara Guide
item.description: Hase-dera in Sakurai is a mountainside ‘temple of flowers’ reached by a long covered stone stairway (noborro) lined with lanterns. Famous for 7,000 peonies in late April and blazing maples in autumn, it also enshrines a towering 10-metre wooden Kannon. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hase, Sakurai, Nara Hours 8:30–17:00 (seasonal) Admission ¥500 Time needed 1–1.

item.title: Heijo Palace Site: Nara's Ancient Capital — Guide
item.description: The Heijo Palace Site is the vast, open remains of the imperial palace of Nara’s 8th-century capital, Heijo-kyo, now a UNESCO World Heritage park. Sweeping lawns are dotted with the grandly reconstructed Suzaku Gate and Daigokuden hall, plus free museums — a spacious, uncrowded counterpoint to the temples. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Sakicho, Nara (west of the center) Hours Grounds always open; buildings 9:00–16:30, closed Mon Admission Free Time needed 1.

item.title: Horyu-ji Temple: World's Oldest Wooden Building — Nara Guide
item.description: Horyu-ji in Ikaruga, founded by Prince Shotoku in 607, preserves the oldest surviving wooden buildings on earth and was Japan’s first UNESCO World Heritage listing. Its serene precinct of pagoda, golden hall and treasure galleries is a quieter, deeply historic alternative to central Nara. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Ikaruga, Nara Pref. (SW of Nara city) Hours 8:00–17:00 (to 16:30 winter) Admission ¥1,500 (all three areas) Time needed 1.

item.title: Isuien & Yoshikien Gardens: Nara's Best Gardens — Guide
item.description: Just north of Nara Park sit two of the city’s loveliest strolling gardens. Isuien is a refined pond garden that ‘borrows’ the scenery of Todai-ji’s gate and the eastern hills, while neighbouring Yoshikien offers three gardens — pond, moss and tea-flower — and is free to foreign visitors. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Suimoncho, Nara (near Todai-ji) Hours 9:30–16:30 (Isuien closed Tue); Yoshikien ~9:00–17:00 Admission Isuien ¥1,200; Yoshikien free for foreign visitors Time needed 1 hour for both Best time Fresh green (May) & autumn maples What to See Isuien — a two-part pond garden framing Todai-ji’s Nandaimon and Mt.

item.title: Kakinoha-zushi: Persimmon-Leaf Sushi — Nara Food Guide
item.description: Kakinoha-zushi is Nara’s signature sushi: bite-sized pressed pieces of mackerel or salmon wrapped in aromatic persimmon leaves. Born as a mountain-country way to preserve fish, its subtle leaf fragrance and firm texture make it both a beloved local meal and a perfect travel snack or souvenir. 🗓️ At a Glance Where Shops citywide; Yoshino & Nara Station area Type Pressed sushi (saba/salmon) Price ~¥800–1,500 per box Eat Room temperature; keeps well Best for Lunch, picnics, souvenirs What to Know Classic fillings are mackerel (saba) and salmon; the leaf is not eaten.

item.title: Kashihara Shrine: Japan's First Emperor — Nara Guide
item.description: Kashihara Jingu is a grand Meiji-era shrine at the foot of Mt. Unebi, dedicated to Japan’s legendary first emperor, Jimmu. Its wide gravel approaches, cypress halls and forested grounds make it one of Nara’s most spacious and dignified shrines, hugely popular for New Year prayers. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Kashihara, Nara Hours Grounds sunrise–sunset; office ~9:00–17:00 Admission Free Time needed 1 hour Best time New Year (hatsumode); spring What to See The vast outer hall (Gaihaiden) and cypress architecture in classic shrine style.

item.title: Kasuga Mantoro: 3,000 Lanterns Lit — Nara Festival Guide
item.description: Twice a year, all 3,000 bronze and stone lanterns of Kasuga Taisha are lit at once for the Mantoro festival, filling the shrine and its forest approach with a magical golden glow. Held in early February (Setsubun) and mid-August (Chugen), it’s one of Nara’s most atmospheric evenings. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Kasuga Taisha, Nara Park Dates Setsubun (early Feb) & Chugen (14–15 Aug) Admission Small special-entry fee in the evening Time needed 1–1.

item.title: Kasuga Taisha Shrine: Lanterns, Forest & Nara Guide
item.description: Kasuga Taisha is Nara’s grand vermilion shrine, founded in 768 and famous for some 3,000 bronze and stone lanterns lining its halls and forest approach. A UNESCO World Heritage site, it sits at the foot of the sacred, untouched Kasugayama primeval forest. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Kasugano-cho, Nara (Nara Park) Hours 6:30–17:30 (approx., seasonal) Admission Free grounds; ¥500 inner area Time needed 1 hour Best time Lantern festivals (early Feb & mid-Aug) What to See The vermilion main shrine and its corridors hung with hundreds of bronze lanterns.

item.title: Kasugayama Primeval Forest: Sacred Woods Walk — Nara
item.description: Behind Kasuga Taisha rises the Kasugayama Primeval Forest, a sacred woodland protected from logging for over 1,000 years and part of Nara’s UNESCO World Heritage listing. Cool, mossy paths through ancient trees offer a quiet, atmospheric escape right beside the deer park. 🗓️ At a Glance Location East of Nara Park, behind Kasuga Taisha Hours Daylight (paths); avoid dusk Admission Free Time needed 1–2 hours Best time Fresh green (spring) & autumn What to See & Do An ancient protected forest of giant cedars, oaks and ferns, untouched by logging.

item.title: Kofuku-ji Temple & Five-Story Pagoda: Nara Guide
item.description: Kofuku-ji stands at the western edge of Nara Park, its 50-metre five-story pagoda one of the city’s most photographed silhouettes, especially mirrored in nearby Sarusawa Pond. A UNESCO World Heritage temple, its treasure hall holds Japan’s most beloved Buddhist statue, the three-faced Ashura. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Noborioji-cho, Nara Hours 9:00–17:00 (halls) Admission Grounds free; Central Golden Hall ¥500, Treasure Museum ¥700 Time needed 1 hour Best time Sunset for the pagoda What to See The five-story pagoda (1426), Japan’s second-tallest wooden pagoda.

item.title: Mitarai Gorge (Tenkawa): Emerald River Walk — Nara
item.description: Mitarai Gorge in the mountain village of Tenkawa is one of Nara’s most beautiful ravines, a river trail of clear emerald pools, waterfalls and suspension bridges deep in the Kii Mountains. It’s spectacular in fresh green and among Kansai’s finest autumn-foliage walks. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Tenkawa, Yoshino District, Nara Hours Daylight (mountain trail) Admission Free Time needed 2–3 hours (round trail) Best time Fresh green (May); autumn (late Oct–Nov) What to See Vivid emerald river pools and clear cascades along a well-made riverside path.

item.title: Miwa Somen: Nara's Fine Noodles — Food Guide
item.description: Miwa, at the foot of sacred Mt. Miwa, is regarded as the birthplace of Japanese somen. These ultra-fine hand-stretched wheat noodles are eaten chilled with dipping sauce in summer and as warming nyumen in a hot broth in winter — a Nara specialty with over a thousand years of history. 🗓️ At a Glance Where Miwa/Sakurai area & citywide Dish Somen (cold) / Nyumen (hot) Price ~¥800–1,300 a bowl Season Cold in summer; nyumen in winter Best for Light lunch; dried noodles as souvenir What to Know Miwa is the birthplace of somen, hand-stretched to a fine, springy thinness.

item.title: Mt. Ikoma: Retro Cable Car & Night Views — Nara
item.description: Mount Ikoma straddles the Nara–Osaka border and is reached by Japan’s oldest funicular, whose retro cat- and dog-shaped cars delight families. The summit has a nostalgic amusement park and one of Kansai’s great night-view panoramas over the Osaka plain. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Ikoma, Nara (Nara–Osaka border) Hours Cable car daytime–evening; park seasonal Admission Cable car ~¥370 each way; park rides extra Time needed 2–3 hours Best time Clear evenings for night views What to See Japan’s oldest cable car with novelty cat/dog cars — a hit with kids.

item.title: Mt. Odaigahara: Misty Highland Hiking — Nara Guide
item.description: Mount Odaigahara is one of Japan’s rainiest highlands, a plateau of misty forests, moorland and dramatic viewpoints deep in the Kii Mountains. Well-made boardwalk trails make its pristine nature accessible, with the popular East Course reachable by most walkers. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Kamikitayama, Nara Pref. Hours Daylight; road open ~late Apr–late Nov Admission Free Time needed 2–4 hours (East Course) Best time Summer greenery & autumn (Oct) What to See The East Course boardwalk loop past Hidegatake peak and Daijagura cliff viewpoint.

item.title: Mt. Wakakusa & Yamayaki Grass-Burning — Nara Guide
item.description: Mount Wakakusa is a gentle grass-covered hill rising above Nara Park, offering some of the city’s best panoramas and roaming deer on its slopes. Each January its dry grass is dramatically set ablaze in the Wakakusa Yamayaki festival, capped by fireworks. 🗓️ At a Glance Location East edge of Nara Park Hours Open mid-March to mid-December, 9:00–17:00 Admission ¥150 to climb Time needed 1–1.

item.title: Mt. Yoshino Cherry Blossoms: Complete Guide — Nara
item.description: Mount Yoshino (Yoshinoyama) is Japan’s most famous cherry-blossom destination, with some 30,000 trees blanketing the mountainside in four zones that bloom in succession. A UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape, it turns pink for roughly two weeks each April and is unforgettable at dawn. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Yoshino, Nara Pref. Hours Open mountain; shops daytime Admission Free (ropeway ~¥450 one-way) Time needed Half to full day Best time Early–mid April (blossoms) The Four Blossom Zones Shimo Senbon (lower) — first to bloom, near the ropeway and Kimpusen-ji temple.

item.title: Muro-ji Temple: 'Women's Koya' Pagoda — Nara Guide
item.description: Muro-ji is a serene mountain temple in Uda, historically welcoming women when Mt. Koya barred them — earning the name ‘Women’s Koya’. Its exquisite small five-story pagoda amid cedar forest, plus spring rhododendrons and autumn maples, make it one of Nara’s loveliest quiet temples. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Uda, Nara Pref. (east of Nara) Hours 9:00–16:00 (seasonal) Admission ¥600 Time needed 1–1.

item.title: Nakatanidou High-Speed Mochi Pounding — Nara Food Guide
item.description: Nakatanidou is Nara’s most famous mochi shop, celebrated for lightning-fast mochi pounding (kosoku mochitsuki) that draws crowds to its Sanjo-dori storefront. The freshly pounded mugwort mochi (yomogi mochi), filled with sweet red bean, is soft, warm and best eaten on the spot. 🗓️ At a Glance Where Sanjo-dori, near Sarusawa Pond, Nara Item Yomogi mochi with red bean Price ~¥150 each Show Impromptu high-speed pounding daily Best for A quick snack; watching the spectacle What to Know The high-speed pounding show is a Nara icon — arm-blurring speed and shouts.

item.title: Nara Calligraphy, Brushes & Ink: Hands-On Guide
item.description: Nara is a historic center of Japanese writing craft — fine sumi ink (Nara-zumi) and fude brushes have been made here for centuries. Hands-on workshops let you grind ink, learn basic brush strokes and try shodo calligraphy, a calm, screen-free cultural experience amid the temple sightseeing. 🗓️ At a Glance Where Nara city workshops & craft studios Activity Shodo calligraphy; brush/ink craft Price ~¥2,000–3,500 Duration 60–90 min Best for Culture lovers; a calm activity What to Know Nara is famed for Nara-zumi sumi ink and finely made fude brushes.

item.title: Nara Fireflies: Where & When to See Them — Guide
item.description: For a few magical weeks in early summer, fireflies (hotaru) shimmer above Nara’s clear streams and ponds. From spots near Sarusawa Pond to the mountain villages, their soft glow is a fleeting seasonal delight best enjoyed quietly after dark. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Clear streams around Nara & mountain villages Hours After dark, ~19:30–21:00 Admission Free Time needed 1 hour Best time Late May–June Seeing the Fireflies Look along clean streams and rice-paddy edges on warm, windless, moonless nights.

item.title: Nara National Museum: Buddhist Art & Shosoin — Guide
item.description: The Nara National Museum, on the edge of Nara Park, holds one of Japan’s finest collections of Buddhist sculpture and art. Its elegant Meiji-era Nara Hall and modern galleries are best known for the prestigious annual Shosoin Exhibition each autumn, showing imperial treasures from Todai-ji’s 8th-century repository. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Noborioji-cho, Nara Park Hours 9:30–17:00, closed Mondays Admission ¥700 permanent (special exhibitions higher) Time needed 1–1.

item.title: Nara Park Deer: Feeding, Bowing & Safety Guide
item.description: Around 1,000 wild sika deer roam freely through Nara Park, protected as sacred messengers of the gods and famous for bowing to visitors. Feeding them special crackers (shika-senbei) is the city’s signature experience — this guide covers how to do it safely and kindly. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Nara Park (around Todai-ji & Kasuga Taisha) Hours Always open (deer roam freely) Cost Free; shika-senbei ¥200/bundle Time needed 30–60 min Best time Early morning or late afternoon How to Feed the Deer Buy shika-senbei (¥200) from licensed vendors only — never give human food, plastic or paper.

item.title: Nara Persimmons & Yoshino Woodcraft: Food & Craft Guide
item.description: Nara is one of Japan’s top persimmon (kaki) growers, and autumn brings sweet fresh fruit and strings of dried hoshigaki hung under farmhouse eaves. The same Yoshino mountains supply prized cedar and cypress, worked into delicate kumiko lattice — together they make a lovely food-and-craft side to a Nara trip. 🗓️ At a Glance Where Yoshino & rural Nara farms/workshops Experience Persimmon foods; Yoshino woodcraft/kumiko Price Foods cheap; craft workshops ~¥2,000–4,000 Season Persimmons in autumn Best for Autumn visits; craft lovers What to Know Autumn brings fresh kaki and dried hoshigaki — sweet, chewy and photogenic.

item.title: Nara Sake: Birthplace of Refined Sake — Tasting Guide
item.description: Nara is often called the birthplace of modern clear sake, refined by monks at Shoryaku-ji temple over 500 years ago. Historic breweries around Naramachi and the wider prefecture still craft distinctive sake, and tastings make a rewarding grown-up counterpoint to temple sightseeing. 🗓️ At a Glance Where Naramachi breweries & across the prefecture Try Bodaimoto-style & local junmai Tasting Brewery shops & Naramachi bars Season New sake in winter (sugidama turns brown) Best for Evenings; souvenirs What to Know Nara refined the bodaimoto brewing method that shaped clear sake history.

item.title: Nara Tea Ceremony: Matcha Experience Guide
item.description: A tea ceremony is one of the most rewarding cultural experiences in Nara, the ancient capital where refined court culture took shape. In a serene tea room you’ll receive a sweet, whisk your own bowl of matcha, and learn the graceful etiquette of chado — the way of tea. 🗓️ At a Glance Where Nara city tea rooms & cultural venues Activity Matcha tea ceremony (chado) Price ~¥2,000–4,000 Duration 45–60 min Best for Culture lovers; a calm break What to Know You’ll be served a seasonal wagashi sweet, then whisk or receive matcha.

item.title: Naramachi: Old Merchant Town Walking Guide — Nara
item.description: Naramachi is Nara’s atmospheric old merchant quarter, a lattice-fronted maze of Edo- and Meiji-era townhouses (machiya) now filled with craft shops, cafes, small museums and temples. Free to wander, it’s the city’s best area for slow strolling away from the deer crowds. 🗓️ At a Glance Location South of Sarusawa Pond, Nara Hours Streets always open; shops ~10:00–18:00 Admission Free (some museums ¥200–500) Time needed 1.

item.title: Narazuke: Nara's Sake-Lees Pickles — Food Guide
item.description: Narazuke are Nara’s signature pickles: gourds, cucumbers and melons slowly aged in fragrant sake lees until they turn a deep amber and develop a rich, boozy sweetness. A tradition dating back centuries, they’re a distinctive local flavor and a classic edible souvenir. 🗓️ At a Glance Where Naramachi & Nara Station-area shops Type Vegetables aged in sake lees Price ~¥500–1,500 a pack Eat With rice, tea, or as a snack Best for Souvenirs; sake pairing What to Know Vegetables are aged in sake lees for months to years, deepening in color and flavor.

item.title: Omiwa Shrine: Japan's Oldest Shrine & Mt. Miwa — Nara Guide
item.description: Omiwa Shrine (Miwa Myojin) in Sakurai is considered one of Japan’s oldest shrines, worshipping the sacred Mount Miwa itself instead of a built sanctuary. A revered power spot for luck, health and sake brewing, it is fronted by a towering torii visible across the plain. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Miwa, Sakurai, Nara Hours Grounds always open; office ~9:00–17:00 Admission Free Time needed 1 hour (2–3 hrs with Mt.

item.title: Omizutori: Todai-ji's Fire Festival — Nara Guide
item.description: Omizutori is a 1,270-year-old Buddhist rite held every March at Todai-ji’s Nigatsudo hall, best known for the Otaimatsu — giant flaming torches whisked along the hall’s balcony, showering sparks over the crowd for good fortune. It’s Nara’s most dramatic seasonal spectacle. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Nigatsudo hall, Todai-ji, Nara Dates March 1–14 (climax nights vary) Admission Free to watch Time needed 1–1.

item.title: Shika no Tsunokiri: Nara's Deer Antler-Cutting — Guide
item.description: Shika no Tsunokiri is a centuries-old autumn ritual in which Nara’s stags have their antlers safely cut for the community’s safety before rutting season. Held in an arena beside Kasuga Taisha, deer are caught by seko handlers and the antlers removed by a Shinto priest — a uniquely Nara spectacle. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Roku-en, beside Kasuga Taisha, Nara Dates Weekends & holidays in October Admission ~¥1,000 (arena seating) Time needed 1 hour Best time October (check the year’s schedule) What to Know Stags' antlers are cut each autumn for public safety before the rut.

item.title: Soni Highland (Soni Kogen): Golden Pampas Grass — Nara
item.description: Soni Highland (Soni Kogen) is a rolling upland famed for silver pampas grass (susuki) that turns golden and glows in the low autumn sun. Easy plateau trails and a photogenic marsh make it one of Kansai’s most beloved autumn landscapes. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Soni village, Nara Pref. Hours Open plateau (daylight) Admission Free (parking fee) Time needed 1.

item.title: Tanzan Shrine: Wooden Pagoda & Autumn Leaves — Nara
item.description: Tanzan Shrine, tucked in the hills of Sakurai, is famed for Japan’s only thirteen-story wooden pagoda and for the historic meeting that sparked the Taika Reforms. Framed by around 3,000 maples, it is one of Nara’s most beautiful autumn-foliage shrines. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Tanzan, Sakurai, Nara Hours 8:30–16:30 Admission ¥600 Time needed 1 hour Best time Autumn leaves (mid–late November) What to See The unique thirteen-story wooden pagoda, the only one of its kind.

item.title: Todai-ji Temple & the Great Buddha: Complete Nara Guide
item.description: Todai-ji is Nara’s defining sight: a UNESCO World Heritage temple housing the 15-metre bronze Great Buddha (Daibutsu) inside the Daibutsuden, one of the world’s largest wooden buildings. Founded in 752, it sits within Nara Park where sacred deer roam freely. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Zoshi-cho, Nara (Nara Park) Hours 7:30–17:30 (seasonal variation) Admission ¥800 Daibutsuden (¥1,200 combo with museum) Time needed 1–1.

item.title: Toshodai-ji Temple: Ganjin's Golden Hall — Nara Guide
item.description: Toshodai-ji, founded in 759 by the blind Chinese monk Ganjin, is a UNESCO World Heritage temple treasured for its majestic Nara-period Golden Hall (Kondo) — the archetype of classical Japanese temple architecture. Its calm, tree-shaded grounds are a serene contrast to central Nara. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Nishinokyo, Nara Hours 8:30–17:00 Admission ¥1,000 Time needed 45–60 min Best time Combined with Yakushi-ji What to See The Kondo (Golden Hall), a National Treasure and model of classical temple design.

item.title: Yakushi-ji Temple & East Pagoda: Nara Guide
item.description: Yakushi-ji in Nishinokyo is a UNESCO World Heritage temple famed for its 8th-century East Pagoda — long praised as ‘frozen music’ for its rhythmic tiered roofs — and its bronze Yakushi (Medicine Buddha) triad. It pairs naturally with nearby Toshodai-ji for a half-day away from the deer. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Nishinokyo, Nara Hours 8:30–17:00 Admission ¥1,100 (higher during special openings) Time needed 1 hour Best time Morning, combined with Toshodai-ji What to See The original 8th-century East Pagoda, restored and rhythmic with ‘skirt’ roofs.

item.title: Yamato Tea: Nara's Highland Green Tea — Guide
item.description: Yamato tea is grown on the cool highlands of eastern Nara, producing fragrant sencha and roasted hojicha with a clean, mellow character. Terraced tea fields, farm cafes and tasting experiences make it a relaxing, scenic side to a Nara trip beyond the temples. 🗓️ At a Glance Where Eastern Nara highlands (Tsukigase, Yamazoe, etc.) Try Sencha, hojicha, matcha sweets Price Cafes ¥500–1,200; leaves as souvenirs Season New tea in late spring Best for Relaxed cafe stops; souvenirs What to Know Highland-grown green tea with a clean, mellow flavor.

item.title: Yamatokoriyama Goldfish Town: Quirky Nara Guide
item.description: Yamatokoriyama is a castle town that has bred goldfish for over 300 years, and today it wears the fish as its identity — from ponds and shops to quirky goldfish vending machines and a famous summer scooping championship. It’s a fun, offbeat half-day beside a historic castle. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Yamatokoriyama, Nara Pref. Hours Town anytime; shops daytime Admission Free (some attractions small fees) Time needed Half day Best time Summer (scooping championship, Aug) What to See & Do Goldfish everywhere — ponds, shops and even a former phone-box aquarium.

item.title: Yoshino Kuzu: Nara's Silky Kudzu Sweets — Food Guide
item.description: Yoshino kuzu is prized pure kudzu starch, laboriously refined in the Yoshino mountains and used to make some of Japan’s most elegant sweets. Silky, translucent kuzumochi and kuzukiri — best eaten fresh — are a refined Nara treat and a sophisticated edible souvenir. 🗓️ At a Glance Where Yoshino & Nara city sweet shops/cafes Try Kuzumochi, kuzukiri, hot kuzuyu Price ~¥600–1,200 a serving Season Chilled in summer; hot kuzuyu in winter Best for Dessert; refined souvenirs What to Know Kuzumochi — silky, translucent kudzu jelly with kuromitsu syrup and kinako.

item.title: Abashiri Drift Ice Guide: Icebreaker Cruises & Best Time (Feb)
item.description: Each deep winter, the Sea of Okhotsk delivers one of Japan’s most extraordinary natural spectacles to northeast Hokkaido: drift ice (ryūhyō). Vast floes of pack ice — formed far to the north and carried south on the current — crowd the coast around Abashiri and the Shiretoko Peninsula, turning the sea white to the horizon. Visitors get out among it on red icebreaker cruise ships that crunch through the floes, or by ice-walking in a dry suit.

item.title: Akan, Mashu & Kussharo Guide: Eastern Hokkaido Caldera Lakes
item.description: The remote interior of eastern Hokkaido cradles a trio of magnificent caldera lakes within Akan-Mashu National Park — a landscape of crater lakes, volcanoes, steaming earth and deep forest. Lake Akan is famous for its rare spherical marimo algae and a lively onsen town with an Ainu kotan; Lake Mashu is one of the world’s clearest lakes, often wrapped in an ethereal mist; and vast Lake Kussharo offers free lakeside hot springs and sweeping caldera views.

item.title: Akihabara Complete Guide: Electronics, Anime, Maid Cafes & Retro Gaming
item.description: Akihabara exists nowhere else on earth. The district began as a black market for electrical components after World War II, evolved into the world’s largest consumer electronics district in the 1970s, and transformed again in the 1990s into the global capital of anime, manga, and gaming culture. Today it is all three simultaneously: a place where you can buy a server rack, a 1987 Famicom cartridge, a hand-painted anime figure, and a cup of coffee served by a woman in a Victorian maid uniform — all within 500 metres of each other.

item.title: Aoi Matsuri Guide: Kyoto's Elegant Heian Procession
item.description: The Aoi Matsuri is the most elegant and aristocratic of Kyoto’s three great festivals — a serene procession that recreates the courtly world of a thousand years ago. On May 15 each year, more than 500 people in exquisite Heian-period costume, accompanied by horses, ox-drawn carts, and decorations of aoi (hollyhock) leaves, walk in a slow, dignified parade from the Kyoto Imperial Palace to the city’s two ancient Kamo shrines. Without the noise and crowds of summer’s Gion Matsuri, Aoi Matsuri is a living scroll painting — gentle, graceful, and deeply historic.

item.title: Arashiyama Guide: Bamboo Grove, Temples & the Hozu River
item.description: On the western edge of Kyoto, where the city meets forested mountains and the Hozu River, lies Arashiyama — a district that packs a soaring bamboo grove, a UNESCO Zen garden, a monkey mountain, riverboats, a scenic railway, and a famous moon-crossing bridge into one beautiful, walkable area. The towering green corridor of the bamboo grove is the headline image, but Arashiyama rewards a full half-day or more of exploring.

item.title: Asahikawa Winter Festival Guide: Snow Sculptures & Zoo
item.description: Hokkaido’s second city, Asahikawa, is one of Japan’s coldest places — and it embraces winter wholeheartedly. Each February, the Asahikawa Winter Festival raises some of the largest snow sculptures in Japan (it has held world records), with huge snow stages, slides and illuminations along the Ishikari River and downtown. The city is also home to the wildly popular Asahiyama Zoo, famous for its winter penguin walk, and is a hub for Asahikawa-style soy ramen and a gateway to the Daisetsuzan mountains.

item.title: Awamori Guide: Okinawa's Spirit, Tasting & Izakaya
item.description: Awamori is Okinawa’s traditional distilled spirit and the oldest distilled liquor in Japan, with roots reaching back over 500 years to Ryukyu Kingdom trade. Made from long-grain Thai rice and black koji mould unique to Okinawa, it’s stronger and more characterful than mainland shochu. Aged versions, called kusu, mellow over years into something prized and complex. Sipping awamori at an izakaya — neat, on the rocks or in a highball — is one of the great pleasures of an Okinawan evening.

item.title: Boso Flower Fields Guide: Minamiboso Blooms & Access
item.description: Thanks to its mild, frost-free maritime climate, the southern tip of the Boso Peninsula bursts into flower while much of Japan is still cold — making Minamiboso and Tateyama a beloved late-winter and spring flower destination. Along the scenic Boso Flower Line coastal road, fields glow with poppies, rapeseed, stocks and marigolds, and “flower-picking gardens” let visitors pick their own blooms to take home from as early as January. Set between blue Pacific coastline and the green slopes near Mount Nokogiri, the flower fields make a colourful, family-friendly day out and one of the prettiest spring drives near Tokyo.

item.title: Boso Peninsula Cycling Guide: Coastal Routes & Access
item.description: With its mild climate, gentle terrain and long stretches of quiet coast, the Boso Peninsula is one of the best places near Tokyo for cycling. Riders can roll for kilometres beside the Pacific along the Kujukuri coast, climb to flower fields and capes in the south, or pedal sleepy inland lanes past rice paddies and old towns. The famously flat Kujukuri cycling path is ideal for beginners, while the southern Boso’s coastal roads reward stronger riders with sea views and the Boso Flower Line.

item.title: Boso Sea Kayaking Guide: Tours, Caves & Access
item.description: The clear, sheltered waters and rugged little coves of the southern Boso Peninsula make it one of the best places near Tokyo to try sea kayaking. Guided tours paddle out from spots around Tateyama and Minamiboso to explore turquoise coves, slip into sea caves, glide past rocky islets and, on calm days, peer down at fish and coral over the gunwale. Beginner-friendly tours with stable double kayaks and instruction make it accessible to first-timers and families, while the warm Kuroshio current keeps the water inviting from spring through autumn.

item.title: Cape Hedo Guide: Okinawa's Northern Tip, Cliffs & Access
item.description: Cape Hedo (Hedo Misaki) is the wild northernmost point of Okinawa’s main island, where rugged limestone cliffs meet the deep blue of the open sea. A windswept viewpoint with crashing waves below, it offers sweeping panoramas and, on clear days, a glimpse of distant Yoron and Okinoerabu islands to the north. The cape also carries historical weight: a monument here commemorates Okinawa’s 1972 reversion to Japan. Paired with the karst formations of nearby Daisekirinzan and the Yanbaru forest, it’s the grand finale of a northern road trip.

item.title: Chiba Castle Guide: Museum, Cherry Blossoms & Access
item.description: In the heart of Chiba City, Chiba Castle crowns the leafy Inohana hill where the powerful Chiba clan once ruled the region in the medieval era. The handsome white keep you see today is a modern reconstruction housing the Chiba City Folk Museum, which traces the clan’s history and local samurai culture. Surrounded by Inohana Park — one of the city’s best cherry-blossom spots — and close to the venerable Chiba Shrine, it makes an easy, pleasant half-day of history, greenery and city sightseeing right by central Chiba.

item.title: Chiba Peanuts Guide: Japan's Top Peanuts, Sweets & Where to Buy
item.description: Chiba is Japan’s peanut capital, producing the lion’s share of the country’s domestic crop — and “Chiba peanuts” are a prized, premium souvenir nationwide. The sandy soils around Yachimata and the Boso interior yield famously sweet, fragrant nuts that locals enjoy in every form: freshly boiled (yude-rakkasei) in autumn, classic roasted, ground into nutty peanut confections, and even as peanut soft-serve ice cream. From specialty shops and roadside stands to elegant gift boxes, peanuts here are a genuine regional craft.

item.title: Choshi Guide: Cape Inubo, Soy Sauce & Seafood Access
item.description: At the far northeastern tip of Chiba, the port city of Choshi is where the Tone River meets the Pacific — a place famous for three things: soy sauce, seafood and sunrises. Pounded by the open ocean, Cape Inubosaki is one of the first places in mainland Japan to see the New Year’s sunrise, marked by a handsome white lighthouse you can climb. Choshi is also one of Japan’s great soy sauce towns (home to Yamasa and Higeta), where you can tour breweries and taste the difference, and one of its busiest fishing ports, serving superb sashimi and grilled fish.

item.title: Choshi Whale & Dolphin Watching Guide: Tours & Access
item.description: Few people realise you can go whale and dolphin watching within easy reach of Tokyo — but the rich waters off Choshi, where the warm Kuroshio current meets the cold Oyashio off the Boso Peninsula’s northeastern tip, are one of Japan’s most reliable spots. Boat tours head out from Choshi port to look for large pods of dolphins (often hundreds at a time) and, in season, whales such as minke, Bryde’s and even sperm whales.

item.title: Churaumi Aquarium Guide: Tickets, Whale Sharks & Access
item.description: The Okinawa Churaumi Aquarium on the Motobu Peninsula is one of the largest and most spectacular aquariums in the world, and northern Okinawa’s headline attraction. Its centrepiece is the colossal “Kuroshio Sea” tank, where enormous whale sharks and graceful manta rays glide behind one of the planet’s biggest acrylic viewing panels. Set within the seaside Ocean Expo Park, it’s a must-visit for families and anyone heading north, easily combined with beaches, dolphin shows and gardens.

item.title: Daisetsuzan National Park Guide: Hiking, Ropeway & Autumn
item.description: Daisetsuzan is the vast, wild roof of Hokkaido — the island’s largest national park, sometimes called “the playground of the gods” by the Ainu. A sprawling massif of volcanic peaks, alpine meadows, gorges and hot springs, it centres on Asahidake, Hokkaido’s highest mountain (2,291 m). A ropeway whisks visitors into the high country for easy boardwalk strolls or serious hikes, and each September the park lights up with Japan’s earliest autumn colours.

item.title: Dotonbori Guide: Neon, Street Food & the Glico Sign
item.description: No place sums up Osaka’s “eat till you drop” spirit like Dotonbori — a canal lined with giant animated billboards, a forest of neon, mechanical crabs and dragons crawling across shopfronts, and the legendary Glico running man glowing over the water. This is the city’s most famous entertainment and street-food strip, packed with restaurants, izakaya, and food stalls, and at night it becomes a riot of light and crowds. It’s loud, brash, delicious, and unmistakably Osaka.

item.title: Dotonbori Halloween Guide: What It's Really Like in Osaka
item.description: Around October 31, costumed crowds gather in and around Dotonbori for an informal Halloween street party — Osaka’s equivalent of Tokyo’s Shibuya scramble. It’s spontaneous and unofficial: there’s no organised event, no stage, no tickets — just thousands of people in costume filling the Ebisubashi bridge and Dotonbori canalside to see and be seen. It can be fun and photogenic, but it’s also extremely crowded and increasingly managed by police. Here’s an honest picture of what it’s actually like and how to do it sensibly — plus better alternatives.

item.title: Eisa Guide: Okinawa's Drum Dance, Festivals & Where to See It
item.description: Eisa is Okinawa’s electrifying traditional drum-and-dance — rows of performers in vivid costume pounding taiko drums and spinning to the call of the sanshin, all driven by a hypnotic chant and whistle. Rooted in Obon ceremonies to honour ancestral spirits, eisa has grown into a proud symbol of Okinawan identity performed at festivals, cultural parks and street events. The spectacular Okinawa Zento (“All-Island”) Eisa Festival in Okinawa City each autumn is the grandest gathering of all.

item.title: Enoshima Aquarium Guide: Tickets, Highlights & Access
item.description: Right on the Shonan coast facing Enoshima island, the Enoshima Aquarium — affectionately known as “Enosui” — is one of the Tokyo area’s most beloved aquariums, blending marine science with a stunning seaside setting. Its star exhibits showcase Sagami Bay, the deep, biodiverse waters just offshore, in a giant tank teeming with sardines, plus a dreamy jellyfish hall, playful dolphin and sea-lion shows staged against a backdrop of the real ocean and Mt.

item.title: Enoshima Guide: Shrine, Sea Candle & Sunset (Kanagawa)
item.description: A small sacred island linked to the Shonan coast by a bridge, Enoshima is one of the most beloved escapes near Tokyo — a hill of shrines, caves, gardens and sea views topped by a lighthouse-like observation tower. Climb (or ride the outdoor escalators) past the Enoshima Shrine to the Sea Candle, whose deck delivers superb panoramas over Sagami Bay to Mt. Fuji, gorgeous at sunset. Below, the wave-carved Iwaya caves and a lively lane of seafood and grilled-octopus stalls make it a perfect half-day, easily paired with the Shonan beaches.

item.title: Furano & Biei Guide: Flower Fields, Hills & Best Time
item.description: In central Hokkaido, Furano and Biei are the postcard image of the island’s countryside — a gently rolling patchwork of fields that ripple to the horizon beneath big skies and distant mountains. Furano is famous for its summer flower fields, above all the purple sweep of lavender, while neighbouring Biei enchants with sculpted hills, lone trees and the surreal Blue Pond. Whether you drive the panorama roads, cycle the lanes or ride the seasonal train, this is one of Japan’s most beautiful rural landscapes.

item.title: Furano Lavender Guide: Best Time, Farms & Festival (Jul)
item.description: For a few glorious weeks each July, the hills around Furano turn purple as Hokkaido’s famous lavender fields come into bloom — one of Japan’s great summer sights. Rows of fragrant lavender sweep toward the mountains, joined by rainbow ribbons of poppies, salvia and marigolds, all under crisp northern skies. The legendary Farm Tomita leads a cluster of flower farms offering viewing, lavender soft cream and sweets, picking experiences and festivals.

item.title: Fushimi Inari Taisha Guide: Climbing the Thousand Torii Gates
item.description: There is no image of Kyoto more famous than the endless corridor of vermilion torii gates winding up a forested hillside at Fushimi Inari Taisha. Thousands of them — donated over centuries by businesses and individuals — form glowing tunnels that climb the sacred Mount Inari. It is one of the most photographed places in Japan, free to enter, open 24 hours, and far larger and more rewarding than most visitors realise: nearly everyone turns back after the first photogenic stretch, missing the quiet, atmospheric mountain shrine above.

item.title: Gion Guide: Kyoto's Geisha District & How to Visit Respectfully
item.description: Gion is Kyoto’s most famous geisha district — a maze of wooden machiya townhouses, paper-lantern-lit lanes, exclusive tea houses, and willow-lined canals, where the city’s living traditions of music, dance, and hospitality have continued for centuries. At dusk, when the lanterns glow and a geiko (Kyoto’s word for geisha) or maiko (apprentice) hurries to an evening engagement, Gion feels like stepping into another era. It is also a real, working neighbourhood where over-tourism and disrespectful behaviour have caused genuine problems — to the point that some private lanes now ban photography entirely.

item.title: Gion Matsuri Guide: Kyoto's Greatest Festival
item.description: Gion Matsuri is the most famous festival in Japan — a spectacular, month-long celebration that takes over Kyoto every July. Centred on Yasaka Shrine and over 1,150 years old, it culminates in the magnificent Yamaboko Junko, grand processions of towering wooden floats — some over 25 metres tall and weighing several tonnes — hauled through the city by teams of men to the music of flutes, drums, and bells. In the evenings before the processions, the Yoiyama street parties fill the downtown with lantern-lit floats, food stalls, and crowds in yukata.

item.title: Hakodate Christmas Fantasy Guide: Dates, Lights & Access
item.description: Each December, Hakodate’s romantic bayfront glows for Hakodate Christmas Fantasy — a festive waterfront event built around a giant illuminated Christmas tree floating in the harbour. Set against the historic Kanemori Red Brick Warehouses and reflected in the water, the tree (a gift tradition linked to sister-city Halifax) is joined by sparkling illuminations, a nightly light-up “moment,” soup kitchens with hot food, and even fireworks. Combined with Hakodate’s world-famous night view from the mountain, it makes the city a magical place to be in early winter.

item.title: Hakodate Guide: Night View, Morning Market & Access
item.description: A historic port at Hokkaido’s southern tip, Hakodate was one of Japan’s first cities opened to foreign trade, and it wears that heritage beautifully. The headline attraction is the night view from Mt. Hakodate — the glittering, hourglass-shaped cityscape pinched between two bays, rated among Japan’s finest. By day, dig into the bustling morning market for the freshest crab, uni and squid-on-rice, wander the European-flavoured Motomachi slopes, and admire the star-shaped Goryokaku fort.

item.title: Hakone Ekiden Guide: New Year Relay Race & Access
item.description: Every January 2nd and 3rd, the nation stops to watch the Hakone Ekiden — the most beloved and dramatic long-distance relay race in Japan. University teams of runners carry a sash (tasuki) over a gruelling ~217 km round-trip course between Tokyo and Hakone, climbing the steep mountain road past Odawara to Lake Ashi and back. The race is a New Year institution, with millions watching on TV and huge crowds lining the route to cheer the young runners through cold, hills and exhaustion.

item.title: Hakone Guide: Mt. Fuji Views, Ropeway & Lake Ashi
item.description: Hakone is the Tokyo area’s favourite mountain getaway — a volcanic resort region of hot springs, lakes and, on clear days, postcard views of Mt. Fuji. The classic experience is the “Hakone loop,” a fun chain of scenic transport: a switchback mountain railway, a cable car, the Hakone Ropeway soaring over the steaming Owakudani valley, and a pirate-ship cruise across Lake Ashi, where Fuji rises beyond a lakeside torii gate. Add world-class onsen, art museums and easy access from Tokyo, and Hakone is one of Japan’s most rewarding day trips or overnight escapes.

item.title: Hakone Onsen Guide: Best Hot Springs, Ryokan & Access
item.description: Hakone is one of Japan’s premier hot-spring (onsen) resorts — a volcanic region where dozens of springs feed historic inns, luxury ryokan and casual day baths, all just over an hour from Tokyo. Soaking in an open-air rotenburo with mountain or valley views, then dining on a multi-course kaiseki dinner in a riverside ryokan, is the quintessential Hakone experience. With more than a dozen distinct onsen towns, mineral waters of every type, and options from budget day-trips to splurge stays, Hakone is the easiest place near the capital to discover Japan’s bathing culture.

item.title: Hakone Open-Air Museum Guide: Tickets, Art & Access
item.description: The Hakone Open-Air Museum was Japan’s first open-air sculpture park, and it remains one of the most delightful art experiences near Tokyo. Set across a sweeping hillside in the Hakone mountains, it scatters more than 100 sculptures by masters like Henry Moore and Niki de Saint Phalle across lawns, gardens and valley views. Highlights include a dedicated Picasso Pavilion, the stained-glass tower Symphonic Sculpture you can climb, playful works kids can clamber on, and a free hot-spring foot bath to soak tired feet.

item.title: Hamarikyu Gardens Guide: A Tidal Garden Between the Skyscrapers
item.description: Few places capture the strange beauty of Tokyo like Hamarikyu. Step inside the walls of this 300-year-old feudal garden and you’re surrounded by pine forests, a tidal seawater pond, and a teahouse on an island reached by wooden bridges — while directly behind it all loom the glass skyscrapers of the Shiodome business district. The juxtaposition of Edo-era serenity and 21st-century steel, framed in a single view, is one of the most photographed and most quietly moving sights in the city.

item.title: Hatsumode Guide: Tokyo's New Year Shrine Visits Explained
item.description: Every year, in the first three days of January, Japan undergoes a collective ritual unlike anything in most other countries: over 100 million people visit a shrine or temple. Not individually, over the course of a season — but in three days, as a single national event. In Tokyo alone, Meiji Shrine receives more than 3 million visitors between January 1st and 3rd, making it the most-visited shrine in Japan during hatsumode (初詣) — the first shrine visit of the New Year.

item.title: Higashiyama Hanatouro Guide: The Lantern Festival & What Replaced It
item.description: Important update: The Higashiyama Hanatouro festival has ended. Its final edition was held in March 2022, and the organisers concluded the event after roughly two decades. If you came looking for it, this guide explains what it was, why it stopped — and, more usefully, the beautiful evening illuminations and night temple visits you can still enjoy in Higashiyama today. For about twenty years, the Higashiyama Hanatouro (“flower and light path”) transformed eastern Kyoto into a magical evening promenade each March, lining the historic stone streets between Kiyomizu-dera and Maruyama Park with thousands of lanterns and seasonal flower displays.

item.title: Himeyuri Peace Museum Guide: Access & What to Know
item.description: The Himeyuri Peace Memorial Museum in Itoman, in southern Okinawa, tells one of the most moving stories of the Battle of Okinawa (1945). The “Himeyuri” were a group of around 200 teenage schoolgirls and their teachers mobilised as a student nursing corps; most lost their lives in the final weeks of the battle. The museum and adjacent monument, built where many died, preserve their testimonies, photographs and belongings as a powerful plea for peace.

item.title: Hokkaido Autumn Foliage Guide: Best Spots & Time (Sep–Oct)
item.description: Autumn comes first to Hokkaido — Japan’s earliest foliage flames into life on the high peaks in September, weeks ahead of the mainland, before sweeping down to the lakes, valleys and city parks through October. The island’s huge wild landscapes make for spectacular koyo: golden birch and larch, crimson maples and mountain ash against volcanic peaks and mirror-still caldera lakes. From the alpine slopes of Daisetsuzan to the gorges of Sounkyo and the onsen valley of Jozankei, Hokkaido’s autumn is a quieter, wilder counterpoint to Kyoto’s crowds.

item.title: Hokkaido Bear Watching Guide: Where & How to See Brown Bears
item.description: Hokkaido is home to the Ezo brown bear (higuma), Japan’s largest land animal, plus a rich cast of northern wildlife — deer, red foxes, Steller’s sea eagles, red-crowned cranes and whales. Seeing a wild brown bear is a genuine thrill, and Hokkaido offers some of Japan’s best opportunities to do so safely and responsibly, above all from boat cruises along the Shiretoko coast where bears forage on the shore. For guaranteed sightings, well-run bear parks let families get close.

item.title: Hokkaido Cycling Guide: Routes, Best Season & Tips
item.description: With wide skies, long straight roads, light summer traffic and cool air, Hokkaido is Japan’s premier long-distance cycling destination. Cyclists come to roll through the patchwork hills of Biei, the lavender-striped fields of Furano, along dramatic coasts and lakeshores, and into the edges of the national parks. Distances between towns are bigger than elsewhere in Japan, the scenery is constantly spectacular, and a growing network of cycle routes, rental shops and friendly “cycle stations” makes touring a joy.

item.title: Hokkaido Dairy Guide: Milk, Cheese, Soft Cream & Farms
item.description: Hokkaido’s cool climate and vast pastures make it Japan’s dairy heartland, and its rich milk is the foundation of some of the country’s most beloved treats. Travellers come for the famously creamy soft-serve ice cream, fresh milk and drinking yoghurt, artisan cheese and butter, and decadent sweets like Hokkaido cheesecake and caramels. Farm cafés and cheese factories across the island — especially in the Tokachi region — let you taste it all at the source, and even try your hand at cheese or butter making.

item.title: Hokkaido Salmon Fishing Guide: Rivers, Season & Tours
item.description: Salmon are woven into Hokkaido’s culture, cuisine and seasons, and autumn brings one of nature’s great spectacles to the island: the salmon run, when chum and pink salmon surge back from the sea to spawn in the rivers where they were born. For anglers, Hokkaido offers superb shore (surf) and river fishing; for everyone else, watching thousands of salmon battle upstream — or visiting a hatchery and the Sapporo Salmon Museum — is unforgettable.

item.title: Hokkaido Seafood Guide: Crab, Uni, Kaisendon & Where to Eat
item.description: Cold, rich northern seas make Hokkaido a paradise for seafood — arguably the best in Japan. This is the place to feast on sweet king and snow crab, melt-in-the-mouth sea urchin (uni), glistening salmon roe (ikura), plump scallops and the freshest sashimi. The signature way to enjoy it all is a kaisendon — a bowl of rice heaped with a rainbow of raw seafood — devoured at a bustling morning market.

item.title: Hokkaido Snowshoe Guide: Forest Tours, Season & Tips
item.description: For a peaceful, accessible way to experience Hokkaido’s magical winter, strap on snowshoes and walk out into the silent, snow-laden forest. Snowshoeing lets you float over deep powder that would swallow ordinary boots, following guides into birch woods, frozen wetlands and national-park trails far from the crowds. No experience is needed — if you can walk, you can snowshoe — making it perfect for families and first-time winter adventurers. Look for animal tracks, frost-covered trees and frozen waterfalls, and warm up afterwards in an onsen.

item.title: Imamiya Ebisu Festival Guide: Osaka's Toka Ebisu & Lucky Bamboo
item.description: Every January, merchant Osaka prays for a prosperous year at Toka Ebisu, the festival of Imamiya Ebisu Shrine. Over three days around January 10, around a million people pour through the shrine to petition Ebisu, the cheerful god of business and good fortune, and to buy a fukusasa — a lucky bamboo branch hung with golden charms for wealth and success. With its packed lanes, festive stalls, kimono-clad “fukumusume” maidens, and a colourful palanquin parade through the streets, it’s one of Osaka’s most characteristic and energetic festivals, perfectly capturing the city’s merchant soul.

item.title: Imperial Palace Guide: East Gardens, Edo Castle Ruins & Tokyo's Green Heart
item.description: In the very centre of Tokyo, surrounded by the glass towers of Marunouchi and the rush of the financial district, lies a vast island of moats, stone walls, pine forests, and manicured gardens: the Tokyo Imperial Palace, official residence of the Emperor of Japan. This is the site of Edo Castle, once the largest fortress in the world and the seat of the Tokugawa shoguns who ruled Japan for 260 years.

item.title: Isumi Railway Guide: Rapeseed Flowers, Trains & Access
item.description: The Isumi Railway is one of Chiba’s most photogenic country railways — a single-carriage local line winding through the rural heart of the Boso Peninsula. It’s most famous in spring, when the tracks are framed by ribbons of golden rapeseed blossom (nanohana) and pink cherry trees, drawing photographers to capture the little train rolling through a sea of yellow. Cute themed services (including Moomin-decorated trains and a dining “restaurant train”) add to the charm.

item.title: Izumi Nature Park Cherry Blossom Guide: Sakura & Access
item.description: When spring arrives in the rural Boso interior, Izumi Nature Park near Sosa becomes one of Chiba’s loveliest cherry-blossom (sakura) spots — a quiet expanse of ponds, woods and meadows where rows of cherry trees bloom alongside golden rapeseed flowers for a classic pink-and-yellow spring scene. Far from the city crowds, it’s a peaceful place for hanami picnics, gentle walks and birdwatching, and it pairs perfectly with the Isumi Railway, whose little trains roll through the same flower-filled countryside.

item.title: Jidai Matsuri Guide: Kyoto's Festival of the Ages
item.description: Imagine over a thousand years of Japanese history marching past you in a single afternoon. That’s Jidai Matsuri, the “Festival of the Ages” — Kyoto’s grand historical-costume procession held every October 22. Some 2,000 participants in meticulously researched costumes representing every major era from the Heian period to the Meiji Restoration parade through the city in reverse chronological order, a living timeline of Japan’s emperors, samurai, nobles, and famous historical figures.

item.title: Jingisukan Guide: Hokkaido's Grilled Lamb BBQ & Where to Eat
item.description: Jingisukan (“Genghis Khan”) is Hokkaido’s beloved grilled-mutton barbecue, a smoky, sociable feast named for the dome-shaped grill said to resemble a warrior’s helmet. Diners cook lamb or mutton and a pile of vegetables — onions, beansprouts, cabbage, pumpkin — over the convex iron grill, where juices run down to flavour the veg around the rim. Washed down with ice-cold beer in a summer beer garden or a lively grill house, it’s one of Hokkaido’s most fun and convivial meals.

item.title: Kamakura Festivals Guide: Tsurugaoka Hachimangu & Access
item.description: The ancient samurai capital of Kamakura keeps its warrior heritage alive through a year of vivid festivals centred on Tsurugaoka Hachimangu, the great shrine at the heart of town. The most thrilling is yabusame — mounted archers in full medieval costume galloping down a track, firing arrows at targets — performed at the shrine’s spring and autumn festivals. Around these are portable-shrine processions, traditional dances, the New Year’s first-shrine-visit crowds, and the seaside beach festivals of summer.

item.title: Kamakura Great Buddha Guide: Kotoku-in, Hase & Access
item.description: The serene, weathered Great Buddha of Kamakura (Kamakura Daibutsu) is one of Japan’s most iconic sights — a colossal 13th-century bronze statue of Amida Buddha sitting peacefully in the open air at Kotoku-in temple. Once housed in a great hall that was washed away by a tsunami, the 11.3-metre figure has gazed over the seaside town for some 750 years. Together with the flower-filled Hase-dera temple nearby, it anchors a wonderful half-day in the historic former capital of Kamakura, an easy and rewarding day trip from Tokyo and Yokohama.

item.title: Kamakura Hiking Guide: Daibutsu Trail, Routes & Access
item.description: Beyond its famous temples and Great Buddha, Kamakura hides a network of leafy hiking trails threading through the forested hills that ring the old samurai capital. The best-known, the Daibutsu Trail, links Kita-Kamakura’s temples to the Great Buddha and Zeniarai Benten shrine, while the longer Tenen Trail traces a ridge with sea views. These easy-to-moderate walks let you escape the crowds, pass tucked-away shrines and bamboo, and stitch the town’s highlights together on foot — a refreshing, scenic way to experience Kamakura that combines nature, history and a workout in a single day.

item.title: Kamakura Zazen Guide: Zen Meditation, Temples & Access
item.description: Kamakura is the cradle of Zen Buddhism in Japan — home to the great training monasteries of Kenchoji and Engakuji, founded in the 13th century — which makes it one of the best places for a traveller to try zazen, seated Zen meditation. Several historic temples open their halls to visitors for guided sitting sessions, where you learn the posture, breathing and stillness at the heart of Zen practice, often in a serene hall surrounded by ancient cedars.

item.title: Kashiwa Reysol Guide: J-League Match & Access
item.description: For football fans visiting the Tokyo area, a Kashiwa Reysol match offers one of the most authentic and atmospheric ways to experience Japanese J-League soccer. The club plays at the compact Hitachi Kashiwa Stadium (Sankyo Frontier Kashiwa Stadium) — a rare football-specific ground in Japan where steep, close stands put you right on top of the action, and the passionate “yellow” supporters keep up nonstop drumming, chanting and flag-waving for 90 minutes.

item.title: Katsuura Big Hina Matsuri Guide: Doll Festival & Access
item.description: Every late winter, the seaside town of Katsuura stages one of Japan’s most photogenic doll festivals — the Katsuura Big Hina Matsuri. For Hinamatsuri (the Girls' Day / Doll Festival), the town displays tens of thousands of hina dolls all over town, most spectacularly cascading down the 60 stone steps of Tomisaki Shrine in a tiered pyramid of pink and gold. Lit up in the evenings and set against the fishing-town backdrop, the spectacle draws photographers and families from across the country, making it a magical early-spring day trip on the Boso coast.

item.title: Katsuura Katsuo (Bonito) Guide: What to Eat & Access
item.description: The Boso port of Katsuura lands some of Japan’s finest katsuo (skipjack bonito) — a fish so central to the town that it even shares its name (katsuo-ura). Riding the warm Kuroshio current, fat spring “first bonito” (hatsu-gatsuo) and rich autumn “returning bonito” (modori-gatsuo) come ashore here at their peak. The classic way to enjoy it is katsuo no tataki — fillets seared over straw so the outside is smoky and the inside stays ruby-rare — served with ginger, garlic, and ponzu.

item.title: Katsuura Morning Market & Sashimi Guide: What to Eat & Access
item.description: The fishing town of Katsuura on the Boso coast is a paradise for seafood lovers, home to one of Japan’s three great morning markets — a tradition running for over 400 years. Each morning, stalls along the old streets brim with the night’s catch, vegetables and pickles, and nearby diners serve glistening sashimi rice bowls and set meals built around the day’s freshest fish straight off the boats. Katsuura is also the surprising birthplace of fiery Katsuura tantanmen, a local spicy ramen.

item.title: Kerama Islands Guide: Ferries, Snorkelling & Beaches
item.description: A short ferry ride west of Naha, the Kerama Islands are a national park famed for some of the clearest, most luminous water in Japan — a turquoise so distinctive it has its own name, “Kerama Blue.” With brilliant coral reefs, sea turtles, and powder-white beaches, the islands (chiefly Zamami, Aka and Tokashiki) are a snorkelling and diving paradise, doable as a day trip or an overnight escape. They’re also a winter whale-watching spot.

item.title: Kinkaku-ji Guide: Kyoto's Golden Pavilion
item.description: A three-storey pavilion covered in pure gold leaf, mirrored perfectly in the still pond before it, framed by pines and — if you’re lucky — dusted with snow or backed by autumn maples: Kinkaku-ji is the postcard image of Kyoto, and one of the few sights that genuinely lives up to it. The Golden Pavilion shimmers whether under bright sun, soft cloud, or a rare winter snowfall, and the moment you round the path and it appears across the water is unforgettable.

item.title: Kisarazu Fireworks Guide: Summer Hanabi & Access
item.description: Each summer, the bayside city of Kisarazu lights up the night with one of inner Tokyo Bay’s biggest fireworks festivals (hanabi) — a beloved August tradition that sends tens of thousands of shells bursting over the water. Held along the Kisarazu waterfront near the foot of the Aqua-Line, the display reflects spectacularly off the bay and draws huge crowds in summer yukata to picnic, snack at festival stalls and watch the sky erupt in colour.

item.title: Kiyomizu-dera Guide: The Temple on Stilts Above Kyoto
item.description: Perched on the wooded slopes of Higashiyama, Kiyomizu-dera juts out over the hillside on a vast wooden stage held up by enormous pillars — built, famously, without a single nail. From the stage you look out over a sea of maple and cherry trees to the rooftops of Kyoto beyond. It is one of Japan’s most beloved temples, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the climax of the most atmospheric temple approach in the city: the stone-paved, shop-lined slopes of Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka.

item.title: Koenji Awa Odori Guide: Tokyo's Biggest Summer Dance Festival
item.description: For two evenings every August, the laid-back western Tokyo neighbourhood of Koenji erupts into the city’s largest and most exhilarating dance festival. Some 10,000 dancers in traditional costume pour through the streets to the hypnotic, driving rhythm of shamisen, taiko drums, and flutes, while up to a million spectators line the route. This is the Koenji Awa Odori — the biggest awa odori celebration outside its birthplace in Tokushima, and one of the great experiences of a Tokyo summer.

item.title: Kokusai-dori Guide: Shopping, Eats & Access (Naha)
item.description: Kokusai-dori (“International Street”) is Naha’s bustling main thoroughfare — a roughly 1.6 km stretch lined with souvenir shops, restaurants, izakaya, cafés and street performers. Rebuilt in the years after WWII and nicknamed the “Miracle Mile,” it’s the liveliest place in Okinawa to shop for local crafts and snacks, sample Okinawan cuisine, and feel the island’s easygoing energy. Dip into the covered market arcades just off the main drag for a more local, atmospheric experience.

item.title: Kujukuri Beach Guide: Japan's Longest Beach & Access
item.description: Stretching some 60 kilometres in a near-straight line down Chiba’s Pacific coast, Kujukuri Beach is one of the longest beaches in Japan — an immense ribbon of sand, surf and big sky. Its name (“99 ri”) nods to its legendary length, and its open eastern aspect makes it a famous spot to watch the sunrise over the ocean. Long a centre of the iwashi (sardine) fishing industry, today it’s a summer playground for swimming, surfing, beachcombing and seaside seafood, with a refreshingly wild, uncommercialised feel.

item.title: Kujukuri Surfing Guide: Beaches, Lessons & Access
item.description: Chiba’s Pacific-facing Kujukuri coast is one of the Tokyo area’s great surfing zones — a 60-kilometre run of open sand that catches consistent ocean swell from multiple directions. Towns like Ichinomiya (host to Olympic surfing in 2021), Katakai and Taito are packed with surf shops, schools and a laid-back board culture, making it an excellent place to learn or to chase clean waves close to the capital. With sandy beach breaks suited to beginners, lessons and rentals readily available, and reliable surf from spring through autumn, Kujukuri is where many Tokyoites learn to ride — and a fun, sporty addition to a Chiba coast trip.

item.title: Kurama & Kibune Guide: Mountain Shrines, Onsen & Riverside Dining
item.description: Just half an hour north of the city, the mountain villages of Kurama and Kibune offer one of Kyoto’s most rewarding escapes: a sacred mountain temple, a beautiful ridge hike through ancient cedar forest, a romantic shrine of vermilion lanterns climbing a hillside, riverside dining on platforms built over a rushing stream, and a hot spring to soak tired legs. Linked by a forest trail over the mountain between them, Kurama and Kibune are best done together as a single magical day trip — and they feel a world away from the temple crowds of central Kyoto.

item.title: Kuromon Ichiba Market Guide: Osaka's Kitchen, Stall by Stall
item.description: Known as “Osaka’s Kitchen,” Kuromon Ichiba has fed the city for nearly 200 years — a 600-metre covered arcade of around 150 stalls and shops selling the freshest seafood, wagyu, fruit, pickles, and street snacks in Minami. Once the wholesale market that supplied Osaka’s restaurants, it’s now equal parts working market and food-lover’s playground: vendors grill scallops and fugu to order, slice tuna sashimi before your eyes, and torch wagyu skewers at the counter.

item.title: Kushikatsu Guide: Osaka's Deep-Fried Skewers & the No-Double-Dip Rule
item.description: Kushikatsu — skewers of meat, seafood, and vegetables, breaded, deep-fried to a golden crunch, and dunked in a tangy communal sauce — is one of Osaka’s great comfort foods and the pride of the retro Shinsekai district. Cheap, crispy, endlessly varied, and washed down with cold beer, it’s working-class Osaka eating at its most fun. It also comes with the city’s single most famous food rule: no double-dipping. This guide explains what kushikatsu is, the all-important sauce etiquette, what to order, and where to eat it.

item.title: Kyoto Autumn Foliage Guide: The Best Momiji Spots & Timing
item.description: Autumn may be Kyoto at its most beautiful. For a few magical weeks each November, the city’s maples (momiji) turn fiery red, orange, and gold, setting temple halls, gardens, hillsides, and rivers ablaze with colour. The Japanese love of koyo (autumn leaves) rivals their devotion to cherry blossom, and Kyoto — with its hundreds of temples framed by maples — is the country’s premier destination to enjoy it. This guide covers when the foliage peaks, the very best places to see it, the spectacular night illuminations, and how to plan around the considerable crowds.

item.title: Kyoto Cooking Class Guide: Learn Japanese Home Cooking
item.description: A cooking class is one of the most rewarding things a food-loving visitor can do in Kyoto — and one of the few souvenirs you can take home and use forever. In a few hours, a friendly local instructor teaches you to make real Japanese home cooking — washoku staples, Kyoto’s vegetable-forward obanzai, sushi, ramen, or delicate wagashi sweets — often after a guided shop through Nishiki Market to choose your ingredients.

item.title: Kyoto Cycling Guide: Exploring the City by Bike
item.description: Kyoto is one of Japan’s best cities to explore by bicycle. It’s flat, compact, laid out on an easy grid, and dotted with sights close enough together that a bike often beats buses stuck in traffic. Pedalling along the Kamo River with the eastern mountains ahead, then weaving between temples and backstreets, is one of the most freeing and local ways to experience the old capital. This guide covers why cycling works so well here, where to rent, the best routes, and the rules and etiquette you need to know.

item.title: Kyoto Kaiseki Guide: Japan's Haute Cuisine, Explained
item.description: Kaiseki is the pinnacle of Japanese cuisine, and Kyoto is its spiritual home. Born from the refined simplicity of the tea ceremony and the cooking of the imperial court, kaiseki is a multi-course meal that treats food as an art form — each dish a meditation on seasonality, balance, presentation, and restraint. A great kaiseki dinner in Kyoto is not just a meal; it is one of the defining cultural experiences the city offers.

item.title: Kyoto Kimono Rental Guide: Dressing the Part in the Old Capital
item.description: There is no more atmospheric way to explore Kyoto’s historic streets than dressed in a kimono. As you walk the stone lanes of Higashiyama or cross a bridge in Arashiyama, the traditional silhouette transforms the experience — and the photographs. Kimono rental in Kyoto is easy, affordable, and hugely popular with visitors of every nationality and gender: shops dress you head to toe, style your hair, and send you out for the day.

item.title: Kyoto Kodo Guide: The Incense Ceremony, Japan's Subtlest Art
item.description: Alongside the tea ceremony and flower arranging, Japan has a third classical art that few visitors ever discover: kodo (the “way of incense”). In kodo, participants don’t “smell” incense — they “listen” to it, savouring the faint, evolving fragrance of precious heated woods like agarwood with full, meditative attention. Refined among Kyoto’s aristocracy over centuries, kodo is the most subtle and rarefied of the traditional arts, and the city’s historic incense houses offer visitors a rare chance to experience it.

item.title: Kyoto Maiko Makeover Guide: Transform Into a Geiko for a Day
item.description: In Kyoto you can be transformed into a maiko — an apprentice geiko (Kyoto’s word for geisha) — for an afternoon of beautiful photographs. The maiko makeover (henshin, “transformation”) experience is a popular studio activity in which professional artists apply the iconic white makeup, dress you in an elaborate maiko kimono and obi, fit a traditional wig and ornaments, and photograph you in studio or out on Kyoto’s historic streets. It’s a memorable, only-in-Kyoto way to step into one of Japan’s most enduring images of elegance.

item.title: Kyoto Tea Ceremony Guide: Experiencing Chado as a Visitor
item.description: The Japanese tea ceremony (chado, “the way of tea,” also chanoyu) is far more than drinking matcha — it is a centuries-old art of hospitality, mindfulness, and aesthetics in which every gesture, object, and seasonal detail is considered. Kyoto is its heartland: the city is home to the great tea schools that have shaped the practice for centuries, and there is no better place to experience it. For visitors, a tea ceremony offers a quiet, profound window into the Japanese sense of beauty — and many studios now offer warm, beginner-friendly sessions in English.

item.title: Kyoto Yudofu Guide: The Art of Hot Tofu Cuisine
item.description: It sounds almost too simple to be a delicacy: blocks of tofu gently simmered in a clay pot of hot kombu broth, lifted out and dipped in soy sauce with a few condiments. Yet yudofu is one of Kyoto’s most beloved and refined dishes — a quiet celebration of the city’s exceptional tofu, born in the kitchens of its Zen temples. Eaten in a tatami room overlooking a garden, especially on a cold day, a yudofu meal is the essence of Kyoto: understated, seasonal, and built entirely on the quality of one humble ingredient.

item.title: Lake Toya Guide: Showa Shinzan, Onsen & Access
item.description: Lake Toya (Toyako) is a serene, near-circular caldera lake in southwest Hokkaido, ringed by gentle hills and watched over by a pair of very active volcanoes — the lava dome of Showa Shinzan (which rose from a wheat field in the 1940s) and Mt. Usu. A UNESCO Global Geopark, the area pairs lakeside hot-spring resorts with dramatic volcanic scenery, ropeway views, and — every night through the long summer — a fireworks display over the water.

item.title: Makuhari Messe Guide: Events, Expos & Access
item.description: Makuhari Messe, in the Bayfront business district of Chiba, is one of Japan’s largest convention and exhibition centres — and a magnet for international fans of Japanese pop culture. Designed by architect Fumihiko Maki and opened in 1989, its vast halls and event arena host an extraordinary calendar: blockbuster anime, manga and gaming expos, music concerts and festivals, motor and tech trade shows, and major sporting events. For overseas visitors, it’s the venue behind many bucket-list events, and its location between Tokyo and Narita Airport — with a cluster of hotels, malls and a beach park nearby — makes it remarkably convenient to attend.

item.title: Meiji Jingu Guide: Tokyo's Forest Shrine in the Heart of Harajuku
item.description: Step through the towering wooden torii at the edge of Harajuku and the city simply vanishes. Within a few paces the neon, the crowds, and the noise of Tokyo’s busiest youth district give way to a deep, hushed forest — 100,000 trees of 365 species, planted a century ago by volunteers from across Japan. At the centre stands Meiji Jingu, the Shinto shrine dedicated to Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken, and one of the most spiritually significant places in the capital.

item.title: Minato Mirai 21 Guide: Landmark Tower, Views & Access
item.description: Minato Mirai 21 (“Future Port”) is Yokohama’s glittering waterfront district and one of the Tokyo area’s best night-out destinations. Built on reclaimed harbour land, this sleek, futuristic quarter pairs the Landmark Tower — long Japan’s tallest building, with a 69th-floor Sky Garden observatory — with the giant Cosmo Clock 21 Ferris wheel, the historic Red Brick Warehouse, museums, malls and a romantic, illuminated bayfront promenade. Easy to reach and dazzling after dark, it’s the modern face of Yokohama and a perfect complement to the city’s Chinatown and old port heritage.

item.title: Minoo Park Guide: Waterfall, Autumn Leaves & Fried Maple Leaves
item.description: Just half an hour from central Osaka, Minoo Park (Mino-o) is the city’s favourite nature escape — a forested river valley climbing gently to the lovely 33-metre Minoo Waterfall. The paved riverside trail is easy enough for almost anyone, lined with old tea houses and shops, and in November the maples turn the whole gorge brilliant red and gold. It’s also famous for a uniquely Osaka snack: momiji tempura, real maple leaves battered and deep-fried into a sweet, crispy treat.

item.title: Misaki Maguro Guide: Tuna Town, Where to Eat & Access
item.description: At the southern tip of the Miura Peninsula, the fishing port of Misaki is one of Japan’s historic tuna landing harbours — and a paradise for maguro (tuna) lovers. The town built its fame on deep-frozen tuna brought back by long-distance fleets, and today its restaurants serve every part of the fish: glistening maguro-don rice bowls, fatty otoro sashimi, grilled cheeks, simmered collar and even tuna croquettes. Reached by a popular discount “tuna ticket,” Misaki makes a delicious, breezy day trip combining a fishing-town atmosphere, fresh seafood and the wild Miura coast.

item.title: Miura Peninsula Guide: Beaches, Capes & Access
item.description: Jutting into the sea south of Yokohama, the Miura Peninsula is Kanagawa’s breezy coastal escape — a rural finger of land ringed by beaches, fishing ports, sea cliffs and flower fields, all within easy reach of Tokyo. At its tip sits Misaki, a famous tuna port, and the rugged little island of Jogashima with its lighthouse and walking trails. In between are swimming beaches, the science-museum coast of Aburatsubo, seasonal blooms and farm stands piled with Miura’s prized vegetables.

item.title: Miyako Islands Guide: Beaches, Irabu Bridge & Access
item.description: The Miyako Islands, about 300 km southwest of Okinawa’s main island, are a flat coral paradise ringed by some of Japan’s most beautiful beaches. The water — “Miyako Blue” — is dazzlingly clear, and the islands are famously linked by long, scenic free bridges, including the Irabu Bridge, the longest toll-free bridge in Japan. With star-sand beaches like Yonaha Maehama, superb snorkelling and a laid-back pace, Miyako is a dream beach destination reached by a short flight.

item.title: Mount Nokogiri Guide: Hell Lookout, Great Buddha & Access
item.description: Rising straight from the sea on the Boso Peninsula, Mount Nokogiri (Nokogiri-yama, “Saw Mountain”) is one of Chiba’s most spectacular day trips — a former quarry whose jagged, sawtooth cliffs now host the sprawling temple grounds of Nihon-ji. Here you’ll find the thrilling Jigoku-nozoki (“Hell Lookout”), an overhanging rock platform with a dizzying drop and sweeping views over Tokyo Bay to Mt. Fuji, plus Japan’s largest pre-modern stone Buddha, the serene 31-metre Nihon-ji Daibutsu, and the moss-covered ranks of the Thousand Buddhas.

item.title: Mount Oyama Guide: Cable Car, Afuri Shrine & Access
item.description: Rising at the eastern edge of the Tanzawa range, Mount Oyama (1,252 m) has been a place of worship and pilgrimage for centuries — and today it’s one of the most accessible and rewarding half-day mountains near Tokyo. A nostalgic shopping street of tofu restaurants and inns leads to a cable car that climbs to Afuri Shrine, with sweeping views over the Kanto Plain and, on clear days, the sea and Mt.

item.title: Mount Takao Guide: Tokyo's Best Day Hike with Mt. Fuji Views
item.description: Less than an hour from the neon of Shinjuku, a forested 599-metre mountain rises out of Tokyo’s western suburbs and offers, on a clear day, a view of Mount Fuji floating on the horizon. Mount Takao (Takao-san) is the most-climbed mountain in the world — over three million people a year — and for good reason: it’s astonishingly accessible, suits every fitness level from sneaker-wearing tourists to serious hikers, holds a thousand-year-old mountain temple, and rewards you at the bottom with a beer garden.

item.title: Mt. Kongo & Chihaya Guide: Osaka's Highest Peak & Hiking
item.description: On the border of Osaka and Nara rises Mt. Kongo (Kongo-san), at 1,125 metres the highest peak associated with Osaka and one of the region’s most-loved hiking mountains. Famous for a climber who has ascended it over ten thousand times, its well-marked trails draw walkers year-round — wildflowers and fresh green in the warmer months, and a magical coating of juhyo (rime frost) and snow in winter. From the forested ridge near the top you look out over the Osaka plain and Nara basin.

item.title: Naha Great Tug-of-War Guide: Dates, Giant Rope & Access
