item.description: The Naha Great Tug-of-War (Naha Otsunahiki) is one of Okinawa’s most extraordinary spectacles — a centuries-old festival in which tens of thousands of people heave on a colossal rice-straw rope right down the middle of Naha’s main avenue. The rope is so enormous (around 200 m long and 40+ tonnes) that it holds a Guinness World Record, and pulling it is said to bring good fortune. Held over the October sports-day weekend, the festival also features parades, eisa and fireworks, drawing huge, joyful crowds.

item.title: Naha Hari Guide: Okinawa's Dragon Boat Race & Dates
item.description: The Naha Hari (Haarii) is one of Okinawa’s great seasonal spectacles — a colourful dragon boat festival held at Naha Port over Golden Week (May 3–5). Crews paddle ornate dragon-prowed boats called haarii-bune in thunderous races that pray for maritime safety and a good catch, a tradition with centuries-old roots and Chinese ties. With races, food stalls, music and fireworks, it’s a lively, family-friendly festival and a great reason to be in Naha in early May.

item.title: Naha Marathon Guide: Date, Course & Entry
item.description: The Naha Marathon is one of Japan’s most popular and warmly welcoming road races — a full marathon held each December under Okinawa’s mild winter skies. Tens of thousands of runners loop from central Naha through the southern part of the island, cheered on by legendary local support: residents line the route handing out snacks, awamori and high-fives in true Okinawan style. With a sub-tropical climate and festive atmosphere, it’s a bucket-list race for runners and a fun spectacle for visitors.

item.title: Nakanoshima Guide: Osaka's Riverside Island of Art & Architecture
item.description: A long, slender island between two rivers in the heart of Osaka, Nakanoshima is the city’s most refined district — a calm, green ribbon of historic architecture, art museums, and riverside promenades that feels worlds away from the noise of Minami. Here the stately red-brick Osaka City Central Public Hall anchors a cluster of galleries, a famous rose garden, leafy walkways, and stylish waterside cafes. It’s where Osaka comes to slow down, stroll, and look at art and the water.

item.title: Namba & Shinsaibashi Guide: Osaka's Shopping & Nightlife Heart
item.description: If Umeda is Osaka’s polished northern hub, Namba and Shinsaibashi are the buzzing southern heart — Minami — where the city shops, eats, and plays late into the night. A continuous web of covered arcades, brand boutiques, depachika food halls, vintage and youth-fashion streets, and the neon of Dotonbori all link together here in a walkable, endlessly energetic sprawl. Whether you want luxury labels, cheap fashion, electronics, or just to ride the wave of the crowd, this is where Osaka’s pulse beats hardest.

item.title: Narita Unagi Guide: Best Eel Restaurants & Access
item.description: The temple town of Narita is one of the best places near Tokyo to feast on unagi (freshwater eel) — a tradition stretching back centuries to feed pilgrims visiting Narita-san. Along the atmospheric Omotesando approach to the temple, dozens of long-established eel restaurants fillet, skewer and grill eel fresh to order, often in full view of the street, then glaze it in sweet-savoury tare sauce over rice as unadon or unaju.

item.title: Narita-san Shinshoji Temple Guide: Access from the Airport & Tips
item.description: Just minutes from Narita Airport, Narita-san Shinshoji Temple is one of the most important and atmospheric Buddhist temples in the Tokyo area — the perfect first or last stop on a trip to Japan. Founded in 940 and headquarters of the Shingon Chisan sect, it enshrines Fudo Myo-o, the fierce, flame-wreathed guardian deity, and draws millions of worshippers a year (it ranks among Japan’s busiest for New Year’s visits). Spread across a hillside of grand halls, a soaring pagoda and a tranquil landscaped park, and approached by a charming old street of eel restaurants and souvenir shops, it offers a deep dose of living Japanese tradition right by the airport.

item.title: Naritasan Calligraphy Guide: Shodo Experience & Access
item.description: The temple town of Narita is a wonderful place to try shodo (Japanese calligraphy) — the meditative art of writing characters with brush and ink. Narita-san is home to the Naritasan Calligraphy Museum, one of Japan’s leading museums devoted to the art, and the temple offers shakyo (sutra copying), where visitors trace or brush a Buddhist sutra in quiet concentration as a form of prayer and mindfulness. Hands-on brush workshops let you grind ink, learn the basic strokes and create your own piece to take home.

item.title: Naritasan Setsubun Guide: Bean-Throwing Festival & Access
item.description: Each February 3rd, Narita-san Shinshoji Temple hosts one of Japan’s most famous Setsubun celebrations — the bean-throwing ritual that drives out bad luck and welcomes spring. From a special stage, costumed participants hurl roasted soybeans (and lucky packets) to huge crowds shouting the traditional cry, and Narita-san is renowned for its celebrity guests: famous sumo grand champions, NHK taiga drama actors and other stars take part, drawing big crowds and national TV coverage.

item.title: Nijo Castle Guide: The Shogun's Palace & Nightingale Floors
item.description: Nijo Castle is where the power of the shogun was put on display — and, three centuries later, where it was formally surrendered. Built by the Tokugawa shoguns as their Kyoto residence, it is not a fortress of soaring keeps but a sprawling palace of tatami halls, gold-leaf screens, ornate carved transoms, and gardens, surrounded by moats and stone walls. Walking its Ninomaru Palace — across floors deliberately engineered to “sing” like nightingales to warn of intruders — is one of the most evocative historical experiences in Kyoto, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

item.title: Niseko Guide: Skiing, Powder Snow & Season
item.description: Niseko is Japan’s most famous ski destination and a global byword for powder snow. Blessed with extraordinarily light, abundant “Japow” blown in off the Sea of Japan, this resort area on the flank of Mt. Niseko Annupuri — gazing across to the perfect cone of Mt. Yotei — draws skiers and snowboarders from around the world. Four interconnected ski areas, lively après-ski, world-class dining and superb onsen make it a winter resort like no other, while summer brings rafting, cycling and hiking in cool mountain air.

item.title: Nishijin Textile Guide: Kyoto's Ancient Silk-Weaving District
item.description: For over a thousand years, the looms of Kyoto’s Nishijin district have produced Japan’s most luxurious woven silk — the gorgeous, intricately patterned Nishijin-ori fabric used for the finest kimono and obi. Walk these quiet northwest Kyoto backstreets and you can still hear the clatter of looms in workshops handed down through generations. For visitors, Nishijin offers a chance to watch master weavers at work, see dazzling kimono shows, try weaving yourself, and understand the craft behind the kimono you see all over the city.

item.title: Nishiki Market Guide: Kyoto's Kitchen, Stall by Stall
item.description: For four centuries, “Kyoto’s Kitchen” has run down a single narrow, covered lane in the heart of downtown. Nishiki Market is 400 metres of more than a hundred stalls and shops selling everything that defines Kyoto cuisine: mountain vegetables, dozens of kinds of pickles, fresh tofu and yuba, sweets, knives, tea, dried seafood, and an ever-growing array of street snacks to eat as you go. It is the single best place to taste and understand the ingredients behind Kyoto’s refined food culture.

item.title: Nishiyama Trail Guide: Kyoto's Quiet Western Mountains
item.description: Most visitors never set foot in Nishiyama — the wooded western mountains of Kyoto — and that is exactly its appeal. While the eastern hills heave with tour groups, this quiet range of bamboo forests, hillside temples, and country lanes offers some of the city’s most peaceful temple-going and gentle hiking, crowned by the sprawling mountainside temple of Yoshimine-dera with its sweeping views over the Kyoto basin. For travellers who have already seen the headline sights and want the Kyoto that locals keep for themselves, Nishiyama is a rewarding escape.

item.title: Noboribetsu Onsen Guide: Jigokudani, Baths & Access
item.description: Noboribetsu is Hokkaido’s most famous hot-spring resort, and one of the best in all Japan. Its power source is Jigokudani (“Hell Valley”) — a dramatic, steaming crater of sulphurous vents, bubbling streams and rust-coloured rock that feeds the town’s baths. Noboribetsu is prized for the sheer variety of its waters — nine different spring types in one place — so ryokan and day-use bathhouses offer a soak for every ailment. Easy from Sapporo or on the road to Hakodate, it’s a quintessential Hokkaido onsen experience.

item.title: Nomizo Falls & Kameiwa Cave Guide: Heart of Light & Access
item.description: Hidden in the forested Kiyosumi Gorge of central Boso, Nomizo Falls and the adjacent Kameiwa Cave are home to one of Chiba’s most magical natural sights. On clear mornings in the right season, sunlight streams through the cave’s tunnel-like opening and reflects off the still water below, forming a luminous, near-perfect heart shape that went viral and now draws photographers from across Japan. Even outside those golden moments, the mossy rock arch, gentle waterfall and emerald stream make a serene, fairy-tale woodland scene.

item.title: Obanzai Guide: Kyoto's Home-Style Comfort Cooking
item.description: If kaiseki is Kyoto’s formal art, obanzai is its soul food: the everyday home cooking of Kyoto households, built on local seasonal vegetables, simple techniques, frugality, and quiet good taste. Obanzai is what Kyoto people actually eat at home — small dishes of simmered vegetables, tofu, beans, dried fish, and pickles, made to use ingredients fully and waste nothing. For visitors tired of heavy or touristy food, an obanzai meal is a revelation: gentle, healthy, deeply satisfying, and authentically Kyoto.

item.title: Odaiba Guide: Tokyo Bay's Futuristic Entertainment Island
item.description: Built on reclaimed land in the middle of Tokyo Bay, Odaiba is the city’s vision of the future at play. A monorail glides driverless across the water to an island of vast shopping malls, a life-size Gundam robot, digital art museums, science centres, a sandy beach, and sweeping views of the Rainbow Bridge and the skyline. By day it’s a family-friendly playground; by night the bay lights up and the bridge glows.

item.title: Odawara Castle & Hojo Festival Guide: What to See & Access
item.description: The castle town of Odawara, gateway to Hakone, was once the mighty stronghold of the Hojo clan who ruled much of eastern Japan until Toyotomi Hideyoshi’s famous siege in 1590. Today its handsomely reconstructed castle keep anchors a park of cherry trees and museums, and each spring the town celebrates its samurai past with the Hojo Godai Festival, when costumed warriors, princesses and musicians parade through the streets. Add a moat-side bloom of cherry blossoms, a hilltop view to the sea, and the town’s famous kamaboko fish cake, and Odawara makes a rewarding history stop on the way to Hakone.

item.title: Odawara Kamaboko & Seafood Guide: What to Eat & Access
item.description: The castle town of Odawara, gateway to Hakone, is one of Japan’s great homes of kamaboko — the springy steamed fish cake refined here over centuries thanks to fresh Sagami Bay catch and clean mountain water. Beyond the famous pink-and-white loaves, Odawara serves up fresh fish, grilled age-kama fritters, and a lively port market. Visitors can tour kamaboko makers, taste the difference between artisan and everyday versions, and even make their own at hands-on workshops.

item.title: Okinawa Beaches Guide: West Coast, Manzamo & Resorts
item.description: Okinawa’s west coast is the island’s resort belt — a string of white-sand beaches, turquoise lagoons and clifftop scenery running through Onna Village and beyond. Highlights include the elephant-trunk rock of Cape Manzamo, the calm waters of Manza, and a line of resort beaches perfect for swimming, snorkelling and unforgettable west-facing sunsets. With easy access from Naha and the airport, this coast is where most beach holidays in Okinawa happen.

item.title: Okinawa Cherry Blossoms Guide: Japan's First Sakura (Jan–Feb)
item.description: Okinawa sees Japan’s first cherry blossoms of the year — blooming in January and February, weeks ahead of the mainland. The island’s sakura is the kanhizakura (hikanzakura), a vivid, deep-pink bell-shaped cherry quite different from the pale Somei-Yoshino seen elsewhere. Set against subtropical green and historic castle walls, Okinawa’s early blossoms make for a uniquely warm-weather hanami, celebrated with cherry festivals in the north. It’s a wonderful reason to visit the island in winter.

item.title: Okinawa Diving & Snorkelling Guide: Spots, Trips & Tips
item.description: With warm, gin-clear seas, vast coral reefs and abundant marine life, Okinawa is one of Asia’s great diving and snorkelling destinations. From the dazzling “Kerama Blue” reefs and the glowing Blue Cave off Cape Maeda, to manta cleaning stations and the mysterious Yonaguni Monument, there’s something for every level — including easy trial (“experience”) dives for total beginners and snorkelling trips for non-divers. Operators across the island make it simple to get in the water.

item.title: Okinawa Karate Guide: The Birthplace, Dojos & Experiences
item.description: Okinawa is the birthplace of karate, which grew from the indigenous Ryukyu fighting art “te” blended with Chinese martial influences. For practitioners worldwide, training in Okinawa is a pilgrimage to the source; for travellers, it’s a rare chance to step into a traditional dojo and learn the basics — stances, blocks, strikes and the spirit of respect at the heart of the art. With beginner-friendly experiences and the impressive Okinawa Karate Kaikan, anyone can connect with this living heritage.

item.title: Okinawa Soba Guide: What It Is, Where to Eat & Types
item.description: Despite the name, Okinawa soba contains no buckwheat — it’s a beloved local comfort food of thick, chewy wheat noodles in a clear, savoury pork-and-bonito broth, topped with tender pork, fish cake, pickled ginger and spring onion. Found everywhere from humble shokudo (diners) to dedicated specialists, it’s one of the first tastes of Okinawa most visitors fall for. Regional variations and toppings — from meaty soki to braised rafute — make it endlessly satisfying.

item.title: Okinawan Cuisine Guide: Goya Champuru, Rafute & More
item.description: Okinawan cuisine is a world of its own — shaped by the Ryukyu Kingdom, Chinese and Southeast Asian trade, and a famous longevity food culture. Its signature dish is goya champuru, a stir-fry of bitter melon, tofu, egg and pork that’s both healthy and addictive. Alongside it sit rafute (melting sweet-soy pork belly), tofu dishes, sea vegetables and pork cooked “from snout to tail.” Hearty, distinctive and deeply local, Okinawan home cooking is a highlight of any visit.

item.title: Okutama Guide: Tokyo's Wild Mountain Frontier
item.description: Most people are astonished to learn that Tokyo — the word that means glass towers and 37 million people — also contains genuine mountain wilderness. Travel two hours west of Shinjuku and the metropolis gives way entirely to steep forested valleys, crystal-clear rivers, a turquoise reservoir, and limestone caves: this is Okutama, the mountainous far-western edge of Tokyo Prefecture, part of the Chichibu-Tama-Kai National Park. Here you can kayak on a mountain lake, walk through a gorge, descend into a cave, soak in a hot spring, and stand among some of the Kanto region’s finest autumn colour — all without leaving Tokyo.

item.title: Onjuku & Southern Boso Coast Guide: Beaches & Access
item.description: The breezy resort town of Onjuku, on Chiba’s outer Boso coast, is a classic Japanese seaside escape — a crescent of white sand and turquoise shallows that has drawn beachgoers since the early 20th century. Gentle, clean and family-friendly, Onjuku Beach is great for swimming and lazing, watched over by a quirky “Tsukimi” mermaid statue and a monument commemorating the 1609 rescue of shipwrecked Spanish sailors bound for Mexico (the town’s enduring link to Acapulco).

item.title: Orion Beer Guide: Brewery Tour, Tasting & Access (Nago)
item.description: Orion Beer is Okinawa’s hometown brew — a crisp, easy-drinking lager designed for the island’s heat and humidity, and a fixture of every izakaya table and beach barbecue. Founded in Nago in 1957, Orion is a beloved symbol of Okinawan identity. At the Nago brewery (Orion Happy Park) you can tour the production line and reward yourself with a glass of ultra-fresh draft straight from the source — a fun, family-friendly stop in northern Okinawa, often combined with the aquarium.

item.title: Osaka Aquarium Kaiyukan Guide: Whale Sharks & the Pacific Tank
item.description: The Osaka Aquarium Kaiyukan is one of the largest and most acclaimed aquariums in the world, built around a single breathtaking idea: a colossal central tank representing the Pacific Ocean, nine metres deep, home to whale sharks — the largest fish on Earth — gliding past as you spiral down around it. Rather than a series of separate rooms, Kaiyukan takes you on a journey through the habitats of the Pacific Rim, from rainforest to Antarctic to the open sea.

item.title: Osaka Bay Guide: Kaiyukan, the Ferris Wheel & Sakurajima
item.description: West of the city centre, Osaka Bay opens the metropolis to the sea — a breezy waterfront of attractions, harbour views, and big-sky sunsets that makes a refreshing change from the neon canyons of Minami. Here you’ll find the giant Tempozan Ferris wheel, the superb Kaiyukan aquarium, sightseeing cruises, and, across the water on Sakurajima, Universal Studios Japan. It’s family territory and a great spot to watch the sun sink over the harbour.

item.title: Osaka Castle Guide: The Tower, Park & Best Times to Visit
item.description: Rising on its great stone base above a sea of green, Osaka Castle is the symbol of the city and its single most famous sight. The gleaming white-and-green keep, trimmed with golden tigers and crests, sits within a vast park ringed by massive stone walls and broad moats — a monument to Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the warlord who unified Japan and built his power base here in the 16th century. Today the keep houses a modern museum, the top floor offers sweeping city views, and the surrounding park is one of Osaka’s best spots for cherry and plum blossom.

item.title: Osaka Cherry Blossom Guide: Best Hanami Spots & Timing
item.description: For about two weeks each spring, Osaka turns pink. Cherry blossom (sakura) season transforms the castle moats, riverbanks, and parks into clouds of blossom, and the city throws itself into hanami — flower-viewing picnics under the trees, by day and (lit up) by night. From the iconic combination of blossoms and Osaka Castle to the riverside tunnels of the Kema Sakuranomiya and the once-a-year Japan Mint passage, Osaka has some of the Kansai region’s best and liveliest cherry-blossom spots.

item.title: Osaka Cooking Class & Food Tour Guide: Eat & Cook Like a Local
item.description: Osaka calls itself “the nation’s kitchen” and lives by the motto kuidaore — “eat until you drop.” So there’s no better city to dive into Japanese food hands-on, whether by learning to flip your own takoyaki and griddle okonomiyaki, or by following a local guide through the neon of Dotonbori and the stalls of Kuromon on a food tour. Both turn Osaka’s famous street food from something you eat into something you understand — and they’re sociable, delicious, and genuinely fun.

item.title: Osaka Kendo Class Guide: Try the Way of the Sword
item.description: Behind the thunderous shouts and clashing bamboo of a dojo lies kendo — “the way of the sword,” the modern martial art descended from samurai swordsmanship. A kendo experience class in Osaka lets visitors step onto the dojo floor, grip the bamboo shinai, learn a few basic cuts and stances, and even try on a piece of the armour, all under an instructor who explains the discipline, spirit, and etiquette behind it.

item.title: Osaka Noodles Guide: Kitsune Udon, Kasuudon & Local Ramen
item.description: Osaka is a noodle city, and its signature is udon — soft, slippery wheat noodles in a pale, kelp-and-light-soy dashi that’s gentler and more delicate than Tokyo’s dark broth. This is the birthplace of kitsune udon, the beloved bowl topped with sweet fried tofu, and home to its own quirky specialities like kasuudon. Alongside udon you’ll find rich local ramen, griddle-fried yakisoba, and the late-night noodle shops that keep Osaka fed.

item.title: Osaka Okonomiyaki Guide: The Savoury Pancake, Done the Osaka Way
item.description: Okonomiyaki — literally “grill what you like” — is the hearty, savoury griddle pancake that, with takoyaki and kushikatsu, completes Osaka’s holy trinity of konamon (flour foods). A batter of flour, egg, and mountains of shredded cabbage is mixed with your choice of pork, seafood, or cheese, griddled on a hot teppan, then lacquered with sweet-savoury okonomiyaki sauce, mayonnaise, seaweed, and bonito flakes. Filling, cheap, customisable, and deeply satisfying, it’s Osaka home cooking turned restaurant ritual.

item.title: Osaka Takoyaki Cooking Class Guide: Flip Your Own Octopus Balls
item.description: Eating takoyaki in Osaka is essential — but making it is a different kind of fun. The mesmerising flick-and-turn that shapes runny batter into perfect crisp spheres is genuinely tricky, and a takoyaki-making class lets you try it yourself on a real dimpled pan, with a local teacher guiding your wrist. It’s hands-on, hilarious, and you eat your wonky-but-delicious results at the end — one of Osaka’s most enjoyable and very on-brand experiences for foodies, couples, and families.

item.title: Osaka Takoyaki Guide: The City's Soul Food, Explained
item.description: If Osaka has one defining food, it’s takoyaki — piping-hot, golden balls of savoury batter with a chunk of octopus inside, brushed with sweet-savoury sauce, mayonnaise, and a flurry of dancing bonito flakes. Born in Osaka in the 1930s, takoyaki is the city’s ultimate street snack: cooked on dimpled iron griddles in a hypnotic flipping motion, sold from stalls and specialist shops on nearly every corner of Minami. Crisp outside, molten and creamy inside, it’s Osaka soul food at its purest.

item.title: Osaka Winter Illuminations Guide: Castle Light-Up & City Lights
item.description: When the days shorten, Osaka lights up. From December into February, the city stages some of Japan’s biggest winter illuminations — millions of LEDs turning parks, riverbanks, and boulevards into glowing wonderlands. The headline is the dazzling light show in the grounds of Osaka Castle, but the tree-lined Midosuji avenue, the riverside Hikari-Renaissance on Nakanoshima, and the lights at Universal Studios all make the cold season one of Osaka’s most romantic and photogenic times to visit.

item.title: Otaru Guide: Canal, Glassworks & Day Trip from Sapporo
item.description: A short train ride from Sapporo, Otaru is a postcard-pretty port town built on a once-booming herring and trade economy. Its centrepiece is the Otaru Canal, lined with handsome stone warehouses and Victorian-style gas lamps — impossibly romantic at dusk and magical under winter snow. The old merchant streets now brim with glassblowing studios, music-box shops, sushi counters and sake breweries. Easy to reach and full of charm, Otaru is one of Hokkaido’s most popular day trips.

item.title: Philosopher's Path Guide: Kyoto's Most Beautiful Walk
item.description: The Philosopher’s Path (Tetsugaku-no-michi) is a stone-paved walking trail that follows a cherry-tree-lined canal through the quiet temple district of eastern Kyoto. Named for a famous philosophy professor who walked it daily in meditation on his way to Kyoto University, it strings together some of the city’s loveliest temples, shrines, cafés, and craft shops over about two gentle kilometres. In cherry-blossom season it becomes a tunnel of pink reflected in the water; in autumn, a corridor of red and gold.

item.title: Ryukyu Glass Guide: Glass-Blowing Workshops & Shopping
item.description: Ryukyu glass is one of Okinawa’s most colourful crafts — thick, vivid glassware flecked with playful bubbles, born after WWII when artisans recycled discarded American bottles into beautiful new forms. Today the tradition thrives, and visitors can do more than shop: at studios across the island you can blow your own glass — a cup or small piece in the colours of the Okinawan sea and sky. Hands-on, beginner-friendly and rewarding, it’s one of the most popular craft experiences in Okinawa.

item.title: Ryukyu Gusuku Guide: Zakimi Castle & UNESCO Ruins
item.description: Long before Shuri unified the islands, Okinawa was dotted with gusuku — the fortified castles of rival Ryukyu lords. Several of their dramatic ruins, prized for their flowing, beautifully engineered curved limestone walls, are inscribed together as UNESCO World Heritage (“Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu”). Zakimi Castle in Yomitan is among the most accessible and best preserved, its ramparts open to walk and offering views to the sea.

item.title: Ryukyu Lantern Festival Guide: Dates, Lights & Access
item.description: In the cooler months, Okinawa glows after dark with the Ryukyu Lantern Festival — a winter illumination where thousands of colourful lanterns and light installations transform a recreated Ryukyu village into a dreamy, romantic night scene. Set against red-tiled houses and castle-style gates (most famously at Murasaki Mura in Yomitan), it blends Okinawan and Asian lantern traditions into a magical evening stroll. It’s a lovely seasonal outing for couples, families and photographers.

item.title: Ryukyu Mura Guide: Tickets, Eisa Shows & Access
item.description: Ryukyu Mura is an open-air theme park in Onna, central Okinawa, that recreates the look and life of an old Ryukyu Kingdom village. Relocated traditional houses with red-tiled roofs and guardian shisa, costumed staff, lively eisa drum-and-dance performances, sanshin music and hands-on craft workshops make it an easy, family-friendly introduction to Okinawan culture. It’s a popular stop on the way up the west coast toward the Churaumi Aquarium. This guide covers the village, performances, craft experiences, tickets and how to get there.

item.title: Sagano Scenic Railway Guide: The Romantic Train Through the Gorge
item.description: The Sagano Romantic Train, known affectionately as the Torokko, is a nostalgic open-window sightseeing train that trundles along the cliffs of the Hozu River gorge between Arashiyama and Kameoka. For 25 slow, scenic minutes it follows the river through forested mountains that explode with colour in autumn, froth with cherry blossom in spring, and glow deep green in summer — a beloved Kyoto experience that pairs perfectly with a traditional boat ride back down the same gorge.

item.title: Sanshin Guide: Okinawa's Banjo, Lessons & Where to Hear It
item.description: The sanshin is the soul of Okinawan music — a three-stringed, snakeskin-covered “banjo” whose warm, twanging sound underpins everything from gentle folk ballads to the driving beat of eisa. An ancestor of the mainland shamisen, it has been central to Ryukyu culture for centuries. For visitors, a beginner sanshin lesson is a delightful, hands-on way to connect with the island’s spirit — you’ll learn to hold it, read the kunkunshi notation, and pluck out a simple Okinawan tune in under an hour.

item.title: Sapporo Autumn Fest Guide: Hokkaido Food Festival (Sep)
item.description: Every September, Odori Park fills with the smells of grilling seafood, sizzling meat and fresh produce for the Sapporo Autumn Fest (Sapporo Autumn Festival) — a glorious celebration of Hokkaido’s harvest and one of Japan’s great food events. For several weeks, the park’s blocks become themed gourmet zones showcasing the bounty of the island: crab and scallops, ramen, jingisukan, soup curry, dairy, sweets, sake and local wine, region by region. With long tables, autumn weather and the whole island’s cuisine in one place, it’s a food lover’s dream and a delicious way to round off summer.

item.title: Sapporo Beer Garden Guide: Museum, Beer Hall & Summer
item.description: Sapporo is the birthplace of Japanese beer, and the Sapporo Beer Garden is the place to toast it. Set in a handsome red-brick complex that once brewed the nation’s beer, the site pairs the only Beer Museum in Japan with grand beer halls where the classic Hokkaido feast — all-you-can-eat jingisukan (grilled lamb) with all-you-can-drink beer — has been served for generations. In summer, the city throws an even bigger party: a vast open-air beer garden takes over Odori Park.

item.title: Sapporo Guide: Odori Park, Susukino & Things to Do
item.description: Sapporo, Hokkaido’s vibrant capital and Japan’s fifth-largest city, is the gateway to the north and a destination in its own right. Laid out on an easy American-style grid, it centres on the long green ribbon of Odori Park, runs north to the historic Clock Tower and former government buildings, and south into the neon buzz of Susukino, one of Japan’s great nightlife and dining districts. Add legendary food — miso ramen, soup curry, jingisukan and crab — plus year-round festivals, and Sapporo is the perfect base for exploring Hokkaido.

item.title: Sapporo Ramen Guide: Miso Ramen, Best Shops & How to Eat
item.description: Sapporo is the birthplace of miso ramen, one of Japan’s three great ramen styles — and a bowl built for Hokkaido winters. Rich, hearty and warming, it pairs a deep miso-based pork broth with thick, curly yellow noodles, a slick of lard to keep it piping hot, and toppings like sweetcorn, butter, beansprouts and chashu. Slurping a steaming bowl in a tiny counter shop while snow falls outside is a classic Hokkaido moment.

item.title: Sapporo Snow Festival Guide: Dates, Sites & Tips (Feb)
item.description: The Sapporo Snow Festival (Yuki Matsuri) is Japan’s biggest and most famous winter event, drawing millions to Hokkaido’s capital each February. For about a week, Odori Park becomes a glittering open-air gallery of colossal snow sculptures — towering castles, temples and pop-culture characters — alongside delicate ice sculptures in Susukino and a family snow-play zone at the Tsudome. After dark, the sculptures are spectacularly lit up and projection-mapped. With street food, hot drinks and a magical atmosphere, it’s a bucket-list winter experience.

item.title: Sapporo Soup Curry Guide: What It Is & Where to Eat
item.description: Soup curry is a Sapporo original and one of Hokkaido’s most addictive dishes — a fragrant, spiced, brothy curry that’s worlds apart from the thick Japanese curry-rice found elsewhere. A light but deeply flavoured soup, often built on chicken or seafood stock and a blend of spices, comes brimming with big chunks of Hokkaido vegetables — pumpkin, lotus root, peppers, broccoli — and a hero protein like fall-off-the-bone chicken leg. You choose your spice level and eat it by dipping spoonfuls of rice into the soup.

item.title: Sawara Guide: Little Edo Canal Town, Grand Festival & Access
item.description: The merchant town of Sawara, in Katori, is the jewel of Chiba’s old townscapes — a beautifully preserved “Little Edo” where black-tiled merchant houses, willow trees and stone bridges line the Ono River canal. Once a prosperous river-trade hub, it retains a rare Edo-period atmosphere, best enjoyed on a leisurely boat ride down the canal or a stroll past its old sake breweries and the former home of Ino Tadataka, the surveyor who first mapped Japan accurately.

item.title: Sea Grapes (Umibudo) Guide: Okinawa's Seafood & Where to Eat
item.description: Umibudo (“sea grapes”) are one of Okinawa’s most distinctive delicacies — a bright-green sea vegetable of tiny, caviar-like beads that pop with a fresh, briny crunch in the mouth. Rich in minerals and part of the island’s celebrated longevity diet, they’re served cool with a dipping sauce as a refreshing starter. Alongside other sea vegetables like mozuku and a bounty of tropical fish, sea grapes showcase the clean, ocean-forward side of Okinawan cuisine.

item.title: Sea Turtle Snorkelling Guide: Zamami & Okinawa Tours
item.description: Swimming alongside a wild green sea turtle in Okinawa’s crystal water is a bucket-list moment — and surprisingly attainable. The reefs around Zamami in the Kerama Islands are among the best places in Japan to snorkel with sea turtles, which graze on seagrass close to shore and surface for air right beside swimmers. With easy beach-entry spots and guided tours that know where the turtles feed, it’s an experience open to families and casual snorkellers, not just divers.

item.title: Senso-ji Temple Guide: Asakusa's Ancient Heart from Dawn to Dusk
item.description: Senso-ji is the oldest and most visited temple in Tokyo — but it is also one of the most misunderstood. Millions of visitors pass through the Kaminarimon gate, photograph the giant paper lantern, browse a few stalls on Nakamise-dori, and leave in 20 minutes. Those who stay longer, arrive earlier, or return in the evening discover something different entirely: a living place of worship with 1,400 years of continuous practice, where the incense smoke carries real prayers, and where the early morning light through the five-storey pagoda is among the most beautiful sights in the city.

item.title: Shakotan Peninsula Guide: Cape Kamui, Blue Sea & Uni
item.description: West of Otaru, the rugged Shakotan Peninsula is famous for one thing above all: the colour of its sea. The vivid, jewel-like “Shakotan Blue” glows beneath dramatic cliffs and capes, making this one of Hokkaido’s most beautiful stretches of coast and its only marine park. Walk out to wild Cape Kamui and Cape Shimamui for sweeping ocean views, then feast on the region’s celebrated summer sea urchin (uni), served gloriously fresh on rice.

item.title: Shibuya Guide: The Scramble Crossing & Shibuya Sky from Above
item.description: The Shibuya Scramble Crossing is the image that says “Tokyo” more than any other. When the lights turn red in every direction at once, up to 3,000 people surge across from all sides simultaneously beneath a blaze of giant video screens and neon — and somehow nobody collides. It happens again every couple of minutes, all day and late into the night. Watching it, and crossing it yourself, is a rite of passage on any first visit to the city.

item.title: Shibuya Halloween: What's Really Happening Now (Honest Guide)
item.description: For years, Shibuya’s Halloween was famous as one of the world’s largest spontaneous costume gatherings — tens of thousands of revellers in elaborate outfits flooding the scramble crossing with no organiser, no tickets, just an enormous self-generating street party. If you’ve read older travel guides, that’s the image they sell. Here’s the honest, current reality: Shibuya no longer wants this, and is actively asking people — especially crowds and tourists — to stay away on Halloween.

item.title: Shin-Yokohama Ramen Museum Guide: Tickets & Access
item.description: The Shin-Yokohama Ramen Museum is a food theme park unlike any other — a “ramen amusement park” where you descend into a lovingly recreated 1958 Showa-era streetscape, all flickering neon, retro shopfronts and nostalgic alleys, to slurp your way around Japan’s great regional ramen. Famous shops from Hokkaido to Kyushu (and even overseas) set up here so visitors can taste Sapporo miso, Hakata tonkotsu, Kitakata shoyu and more in one atmospheric basement.

item.title: Shinsekai & Tsutenkaku Guide: Osaka's Retro Heart
item.description: Step into Shinsekai (“New World”) and you step back into a Showa-era Osaka of glowing retro signs, kushikatsu smoke, and cheerful chaos. Built in 1912 around the Tsutenkaku tower — modelled half on Paris’s Eiffel Tower and half on Coney Island — this once-futuristic district fell on hard times and reinvented itself as the city’s most nostalgic, down-to-earth, photogenic neighbourhood. It’s the spiritual home of kushikatsu (deep-fried skewers), presided over by Billiken, the funny-faced god of “things as they ought to be.

item.title: Shiretoko Peninsula Guide: UNESCO Nature, Cruises & Bears
item.description: Jutting into the Sea of Okhotsk at Hokkaido’s far northeast, the Shiretoko Peninsula is one of Japan’s last great wildernesses — a UNESCO World Heritage site where primeval forest, volcanic peaks and a wild coast of cliffs and waterfalls shelter an extraordinary density of wildlife. This is brown bear country, home also to deer, foxes, eagles and, offshore, whales and seals. Explore the Shiretoko Five Lakes, take a nature cruise beneath sea cliffs, and in late winter watch drift ice pack the shore.

item.title: Shonan Coast Guide: Beaches, Enoden & Access
item.description: The Shonan coast is the Tokyo area’s beloved beach playground — a sunny, laid-back stretch of sand and surf running from Kamakura past Enoshima toward Hiratsuka, all under the gaze of Mt. Fuji on clear days. This is where city-dwellers come to swim, surf, cycle and watch the sunset, riding the charming retro Enoden train as it rattles between the sea and old neighbourhoods. With beaches, Enoshima island, fresh shirasu, and an easygoing California-meets-Japan vibe, Shonan is the perfect seaside complement to historic Kamakura.

item.title: Shonan Shirasu Guide: Whitebait Bowls & Where to Eat
item.description: Along Kanagawa’s Shonan coast, the local delicacy is shirasu — tiny, translucent whitebait (baby sardines and anchovies) landed fresh from Sagami Bay. Served gleaming and raw (nama-shirasu) when the boats are out, or gently boiled (kama-age) and piled over rice, it’s the signature taste of a day at Enoshima and the Shonan beaches. A shirasu-don — a bowl of rice heaped with whitebait, perhaps with an egg yolk and ginger — is the dish to seek out, best enjoyed at a seaside diner with the surf in view.

item.title: Shonan Surfing Guide: Beaches, Lessons & Access
item.description: The Shonan coast is the birthplace and beating heart of Japanese surf culture — a sunny stretch of Sagami Bay where Tokyoites have been riding waves for generations. With gentle beach breaks, a string of surf shops and schools, and Mt. Fuji on the horizon, it’s the most accessible place near the capital to learn to surf or paddle out. Beginners can take a lesson and rent a board on the same beach where locals trade waves at dawn, while the laid-back seaside towns of Kugenuma, Katase and Chigasaki keep the whole scene relaxed and welcoming.

item.title: Shuri Castle Guide: Tickets, Reconstruction & Access (Naha)
item.description: Shuri Castle (Shurijō) was the political and ceremonial heart of the Ryukyu Kingdom for some 450 years, and remains Okinawa’s most important historic site. With its distinctive vermilion halls, Chinese- and Japanese-influenced architecture, and hilltop views over Naha, it is a UNESCO World Heritage component (“Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu”). A devastating fire in October 2019 destroyed the main hall (Seiden) and several structures; the castle is now in the midst of a multi-year reconstruction, which has itself become a fascinating thing to witness.

item.title: Spa World Osaka Guide: The Giant Themed Bath Complex
item.description: Beside the retro neon of Shinsekai looms Spa World — a vast, slightly surreal multi-floor bathing complex where you can soak in a Roman bath, a Finnish sauna, an Islamic-tiled pool, a Balinese spa, and a Japanese rotenburo, all under one roof. Part onsen, part water park, part kitsch theme attraction, it’s one of Osaka’s most fun and affordable ways to relax — a place to spend hours bathing, sweating, swimming, and recovering from a day of takoyaki and walking.

item.title: Sumida River Fireworks Guide: Tokyo's Greatest Summer Spectacle
item.description: The Sumida River Fireworks Festival (隅田川花火大会, Sumidagawa Hanabi Taikai) is the oldest and most prestigious fireworks festival in Tokyo, with roots tracing back to 1733. Over 20,000 shells launch across two competing sites along the Sumida River on the last Saturday of July, watched by roughly one million spectators packed onto bridges, riverbanks, rooftops, and into restaurants for miles around. It is one of the definitive Tokyo summer experiences — and also one of the most logistically demanding to attend well.

item.title: Sumiyoshi Matsuri Guide: Osaka's Great Summer Purification Festival
item.description: Held at the end of summer, the Sumiyoshi Matsuri is the grand festival of Sumiyoshi Taisha, one of Osaka’s oldest and most important shrines — and it traditionally closes the city’s festival season each year. Centred on purification and renewal, its highlights are the solemn Nagoshi-no-harae rite, in which participants pass through a great reed ring to cleanse themselves of the year’s impurities, and a boisterous procession that carries a giant mikoshi (portable shrine) across the Yamato River to a related shrine in Sakai.

item.title: Sumiyoshi Taisha Guide: Osaka's Ancient Shrine & Drum Bridge
item.description: The head shrine of some 2,300 Sumiyoshi shrines across Japan, Sumiyoshi Taisha is one of the country’s oldest and most distinctive Shinto sites — founded in the 3rd century, long before Buddhist influence reached Japan, and built in a rare ancient style found nowhere else. Its image is the steep, vermilion Taiko-bashi (drum bridge) arching over a pond, one of Osaka’s most photographed scenes. Revered as a guardian of sea travel and a bringer of good fortune, it draws over two million worshippers at New Year alone.

item.title: Sumo Morning Practice Guide: Watching Keiko at a Tokyo Stable
item.description: There are two ways to see sumo in Tokyo. One is to attend a Grand Tournament (honbasho) — the great public spectacle of ceremony, salt-throwing, and roaring crowds held in Tokyo three times a year. The other is far more intimate and far less known: watching the morning training session (keiko, 稽古) at a sumo stable, where wrestlers practise in near silence, often just a few metres from a small group of guests sitting on cushions.

item.title: Taco Rice Guide: Okinawa's Tex-Mex Soul Food & Where to Eat
item.description: Taco rice is Okinawa’s quintessential fusion comfort food — seasoned taco-style ground beef, shredded lettuce, tomato and cheese piled over a bowl of white rice. Born near the American military bases in the 1980s as a cheap, filling meal for hungry servicemen, it crossed over into local life and is now an Okinawan icon. Hearty, cheap and crowd-pleasing, it’s a delicious window into the island’s deep American cultural layer. This guide covers its origins, what’s in it, where to eat it and how to order.

item.title: Tanzawa Mountains Guide: Hiking, Trails & Access
item.description: Rising in western Kanagawa, the Tanzawa Mountains are one of the most popular hiking ranges within easy reach of Tokyo — a green wall of ridges, valleys and waterfalls protected as a quasi-national park. Well-marked trails, mountain huts and ridgeline views (including Mt. Fuji on clear days) draw weekend hikers in every season, from spring greenery and summer escapes from the heat to fiery autumn colours. The signature climb is Mt.

item.title: teamLab Tokyo Guide: Planets vs. Borderless — Which to Visit
item.description: teamLab is a Tokyo-based art collective whose immersive digital installations have become one of the city’s most sought-after experiences. The art collective creates rooms where projected light, water, mirrors, and sound respond to your presence — flowers bloom where you stand and scatter when you touch them, koi fish swim around your legs and burst into flowers on contact, infinite fields of suspended lights stretch into mirrored darkness. The result is genuinely unlike a conventional museum: there are no paintings on walls, no benches, no “viewing.

item.title: Tenjin Matsuri Guide: Osaka's Great River & Fire Festival
item.description: Held every July, Tenjin Matsuri is one of Japan’s three great festivals (with Kyoto’s Gion Matsuri and Tokyo’s Kanda Matsuri) and the biggest party in Osaka. Over a thousand years old, it honours Sugawara no Michizane, the deity of learning, enshrined at Osaka Tenmangu. The festival builds to a spectacular evening climax on July 25: a grand boat procession (funa-togyo) of around a hundred lantern-lit vessels gliding up and down the Okawa River, accompanied by drums, traditional music, and a fireworks finale reflected in the water.

item.title: Toei Kyoto Studio Park (Uzumasa Eigamura) Guide: Step Into a Samurai Movie
item.description: Part working film studio, part theme park, Toei Kyoto Studio Park (Uzumasa Eigamura) lets you walk straight into a samurai movie. Built around the back-lot sets where countless Japanese period dramas (jidaigeki) have been filmed, it recreates the streets of Edo-period Japan — wooden shopfronts, a Nihonbashi bridge, a red-light district, a courthouse — complete with costumed actors, live ninja and samurai sword shows, and the chance to dress up as a samurai, ninja, or even an oiran courtesan.

item.title: Tokachi Farm Stay Guide: Rural Life, Hot Springs & Access
item.description: The Tokachi plain in eastern Hokkaido is Japan’s breadbasket — an immense patchwork of farms beneath huge skies, centred on the city of Obihiro. Here you can swap the city for a farm stay, sleeping on a working dairy or crop farm, helping with chores, and feasting on just-picked produce, farm dairy and local beef. Tokachi is also home to the rare, amber “moor” hot springs (mojū-onsen) — peat-rich waters found in only a handful of places worldwide — and a famous food culture of sweets, cheese and the local “butadon” pork bowl.

item.title: Tokachi Millennium Forest Guide: Gardens, Tickets & Access
item.description: In the rolling countryside of the Tokachi plain lies the Tokachi Millennium Forest, one of Japan’s most celebrated contemporary gardens. Conceived as a 1,000-year project to reconnect people with nature, it blends manicured garden artistry with the wild Hokkaido landscape — most famously the sculpted, wave-like grass mounds of the Earth Garden and the lush perennial borders of the Meadow Garden, designed by acclaimed plantsman Piet Oudolf. An international garden-design award-winner, it’s a serene, beautiful stop, with goats, cafés, cycling and forest trails to enjoy at a gentle pace.

item.title: Tokyo Cherry Blossom Guide: Best Hanami Spots, Timing & Etiquette
item.description: There is no week in the Japanese calendar more celebrated than sakura season. For about ten days each spring, Tokyo — a city of 14 million people — pivots its entire social life around sitting under trees. Friends, families, and colleagues converge on parks from early morning to claim prime spots, spread blue tarps, and spend the afternoon eating, drinking, and staring upward at a canopy of pale pink that will be completely gone in a week.

item.title: Tokyo Disney Resort Guide: Tickets, Parks & Access
item.description: Despite the name, Tokyo Disney Resort sits in Urayasu, Chiba, on the shore of Tokyo Bay — and it’s one of the world’s most popular theme-park destinations. The resort pairs two distinct parks: Tokyo Disneyland, the classic castle park beloved for its parades and fairy-tale lands, and Tokyo DisneySea, a uniquely Japanese, nautically themed park (found nowhere else) celebrated for its immersive harbours, detailed theming and more grown-up attractions. With resort hotels, the Ikspiari mall and the Disney Resort monorail tying it together, plus famously polished service and seasonal events, it’s an easy, dazzling day (or several) right next to Tokyo.

item.title: Tokyo DisneySea Guide: The World's Most Beautiful Theme Park
item.description: There is only one DisneySea in the world, and it is widely considered the most beautiful theme park ever built. Where other Disney parks aim at whimsy, Tokyo DisneySea aims at atmosphere — seven elaborately themed “ports of call” arranged around a central volcanic lagoon, with a Venetian harbour, an Arabian bazaar, a mysterious Aztec temple, and a 1920s American waterfront, all rendered with a level of detail and craftsmanship that rewards simply walking around as much as riding the rides.

item.title: Tokyo Onsen & Hot Spring Guide: Where to Bathe in the City
item.description: You don’t have to leave Tokyo to soak in a real hot spring. Beneath the city, natural mineral water rises from deep underground, and Tokyo offers everything from elaborate onsen theme parks to humble century-old neighbourhood bathhouses. Whether you want a full day of Edo-themed bathing or a quiet 30-minute soak after a day of sightseeing, this guide points you to the best current options — and explains the etiquette so you can bathe with confidence.

item.title: Tokyo Ramen Cooking Class Guide: Make Your Own Bowl from Scratch
item.description: You can eat extraordinary ramen all over Tokyo — but learning to make it transforms how you understand Japan’s most beloved comfort food. A ramen cooking class takes you behind the steaming counter: building a broth, understanding the four components that define every bowl, hand-preparing the toppings, and finally assembling — and eating — a bowl of ramen you made yourself. It’s hands-on, delicious, conducted in English, and one of the most rewarding food experiences in the city, especially for travellers who want to take a real skill home.

item.title: Tokyo Skytree Guide: Tickets, Best Times & What's Worth It
item.description: At 634 metres, Tokyo Skytree is the tallest tower in Japan and the second-tallest structure in the world. From its observation decks, the sheer scale of the Greater Tokyo conurbation — the largest metropolitan area on Earth, home to 37 million people — spreads out in every direction until it dissolves into haze. On a clear day, Mount Fuji floats on the western horizon. It is the definitive “how big is Tokyo, really?

item.title: Tokyo Sushi Making Class Guide: Learn from a Trained Itamae
item.description: Sushi looks deceptively simple — a slice of fish on a mound of rice — but every element conceals years of craft. In a Tokyo sushi-making class, a trained itamae (sushi chef) reveals those secrets: how to season and handle the rice, how to wield a Japanese knife, and how to shape nigiri and roll maki with the right pressure and form. You leave not only having eaten beautiful sushi you made yourself, but with knife and rice fundamentals that quietly change how you eat — and make — sushi for the rest of your life.

item.title: Tsukiji Outer Market Guide: Tokyo's Greatest Food Morning
item.description: For 83 years, Tsukiji was the largest fish market on Earth — the beating heart of Tokyo’s relationship with seafood, where billions of yen of tuna changed hands before dawn. In 2018 the famous wholesale auctions moved to a modern facility in Toyosu, but here’s what most visitors don’t realise: the part you actually want to visit never left. The bustling Outer Market (Tsukiji Jogai Shijo) — the warren of stalls, knife shops, and tiny restaurants where the public eats — is still right where it always was, still serving some of the freshest, most exciting food in Tokyo, every morning.

item.title: Tsukishima Monja Guide: Tokyo's DIY Griddle Soul Food
item.description: Of all Tokyo’s regional specialities, monjayaki is the one most visitors have never heard of — and the one locals will most enthusiastically send you to try. It’s Tokyo’s own runnier, savoury cousin of Osaka’s okonomiyaki: a loose, dashi-rich batter studded with cabbage and your chosen ingredients, cooked by you on a hot iron griddle built into your table, then scraped up bite by bite with a tiny spatula. It is messy, interactive, deeply local, and genuinely delicious — and the place to eat it is Tsukishima, a small island in the Sumida delta whose Monja Street packs more than 70 monja restaurants into a few atmospheric blocks.

item.title: Uji Matcha & Tea Culture Guide: Kyoto's Green Gold
item.description: Matcha — the vivid green, stone-ground powdered tea whisked into a frothy bowl — is inseparable from Kyoto, and its finest expression comes from Uji, a small city on Kyoto’s southern edge that has been Japan’s most prestigious tea-growing region for some 800 years. Uji matcha is the green gold of Japanese tea: the powder behind the tea ceremony, and the flavour behind an endless parade of Kyoto sweets, from soft-serve to parfaits to delicate wagashi.

item.title: Umeda Sky Building Guide: The Floating Garden Observatory
item.description: One of Osaka’s boldest pieces of architecture, the Umeda Sky Building is two 40-storey towers joined at the top by a doughnut-shaped Floating Garden Observatory seemingly suspended in mid-air. Glass escalators cross the open void between the towers to reach the rooftop, where an open-air deck gives a 360-degree panorama over the whole of Osaka — spectacular at sunset and after dark. Frequently listed among the world’s great buildings, it’s the city’s best skyline viewpoint and an experience in itself.

item.title: Universal Studios Japan Guide: USJ Tickets, Tips & Super Nintendo World
item.description: Universal Studios Japan (USJ) is Osaka’s blockbuster theme park and one of the most visited in the world — home to the game-changing Super Nintendo World, the immersive Wizarding World of Harry Potter, and thrill rides from Hollywood to Jurassic Park. It’s a full, exhilarating day (or two) of rides, shows, and themed lands, and with the right planning you can ride the headliners without spending your whole visit in queues.

item.title: Upopoy Ainu Museum Guide: Tickets, Highlights & Access
item.description: Upopoy (the National Ainu Museum and Park) at Shiraoi is Japan’s flagship centre for the culture of the Ainu, the Indigenous people of Hokkaido and the north. Opened in 2020 on the shore of Lake Poroto, this thoughtful complex tells the Ainu story — their language, beliefs, crafts and connection to nature — long marginalised and now celebrated. With a modern museum, traditional houses, live music and dance, craft demonstrations and hands-on workshops, Upopoy is a moving, eye-opening stop that adds real depth to a Hokkaido trip.

item.title: Yachimun Pottery Guide: Tsuboya Street & Workshops (Naha)
item.description: Yachimun is the Okinawan word for pottery, and the island’s bold, earthy ceramics are among its most beloved crafts. The heart of the tradition is Tsuboya, a historic pottery quarter just off Kokusai-dori in Naha, where a charming stone-paved lane is lined with kilns, studios, galleries and shops. Here you’ll find rustic plates and cups, awamori flasks, and the famous shisa lion-dog guardians. Browsing the lane — or trying the wheel yourself — is a lovely, low-key cultural break in the city.

item.title: Yaeyama Islands Guide: Ishigaki, Iriomote & Taketomi
item.description: Japan’s southwesternmost frontier, the Yaeyama Islands are a tropical archipelago of jungle, coral and old Ryukyu charm — closer to Taiwan than to Tokyo. Gateway island Ishigaki dazzles with the emerald Kabira Bay, while neighbouring Iriomote is a wild, mangrove-and-jungle island roamed by the rare Iriomote cat, and tiny Taketomi preserves a postcard village of red-tiled houses and water-buffalo carts. Linked by quick ferries, the Yaeyama are an island-hopper’s dream.

item.title: Yanbaru Guide: UNESCO Forest, Wildlife & Access
item.description: The lush, mountainous north of Okinawa Island is Yanbaru — a subtropical forest so biodiverse it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage natural site in 2021. Home to rare endemic creatures found nowhere else on Earth, like the flightless Okinawa rail (Yanbaru kuina) and the Okinawa woodpecker, it offers a completely different Okinawa from the beaches: dense green ridges, waterfalls, mangroves and the dramatic karst formations of Daisekirinzan. It’s the island’s premier destination for nature lovers.

item.title: Yoichi Nikka Whisky Distillery Guide: Tour, Tasting & Access
item.description: The Yoichi Nikka Whisky Distillery, on the coast just beyond Otaru, is the birthplace of one of Japan’s most storied whiskies — and a pilgrimage for whisky lovers. Founded in 1934 by Masataka Taketsuru, “the father of Japanese whisky,” who chose Yoichi for its Scotland-like climate, the distillery still uses traditional coal-fired pot stills. The handsome stone-and-ivy grounds (the setting of a famous NHK drama) house the working distillery, a whisky museum and a tasting bar.

item.title: Yokohama Chinatown Cooking Guide: Classes, Tips & Access
item.description: Japan’s biggest Chinatown, in Yokohama, isn’t just for eating — it’s a great place to learn to cook the very dishes that make it famous. Amid the lantern-hung streets and hundreds of restaurants, cooking studios and classes let visitors get hands-on, folding their own dumplings, shumai and steamed buns, or rolling dim sum under a chef’s guidance, before sitting down to eat what they made. It’s a fun, interactive way to dive deeper into Chinatown than a meal alone, take home a new skill, and understand the Cantonese and regional Chinese cuisine that has thrived in Yokohama since the port opened in the 19th century.

item.title: Yokohama Chinatown Guide: Food, Gates & Access
item.description: Yokohama Chinatown (Chukagai) is the largest Chinatown in Japan — and one of the biggest in the world — a vibrant, lantern-strung warren of some 600 shops and restaurants packed into a few colourful blocks. Marked by ornate paifang gates in every direction, it’s a feast for the senses: steaming dim sum, sizzling street snacks, ornate temples and shops bursting with sweets and souvenirs. Born from Yokohama’s opening as a port in 1859, it’s both a culinary destination and a lively cultural quarter, and an essential stop on any Yokohama visit.

item.title: Yokohama Cosmo World Guide: Ferris Wheel, Rides & Access
item.description: In the heart of Yokohama’s Minato Mirai waterfront, Cosmo World is a compact, colourful amusement park crowned by one of the city’s most recognisable landmarks — the Cosmo Clock 21 Ferris wheel. Once the world’s tallest, this 112-metre giant clock-and-wheel glows in shifting colours after dark and offers a slow, romantic ride over the bay, the skyline and the illuminated harbour. Around it spin roller coasters, a splashy water ride and family attractions.

item.title: Yokohama Fireworks Guide: Summer Hanabi, Spots & Access
item.description: There are few sights more magical than fireworks (hanabi) bursting over Yokohama’s Minato Mirai skyline, their colours mirrored in the bay beside the glowing Ferris wheel and illuminated towers. Summer is firework season across Japan, and Yokohama’s waterfront — with its open harbour, parks and promenades — makes one of the country’s most photogenic backdrops. From large bay-side festivals to special event displays, tens of thousands gather on warm evenings in yukata to watch the sky light up.

item.title: Yokohama Hakkeijima Sea Paradise Guide: Tickets & Access
item.description: On its own island in Yokohama Bay, Hakkeijima Sea Paradise is a one-of-a-kind resort that fuses a major aquarium complex with an amusement park, shops and restaurants — a full day out for families and couples. Four themed aquariums house some 700 marine species, from whale sharks to penguins, with lively dolphin and sea-lion shows, while thrill-seekers ride a surf coaster that races out over the sea, a tall free-fall tower and a giant Ferris wheel.

item.title: Yokohama Ie-kei Ramen Guide: What It Is & Where to Eat
item.description: Ie-kei (iekei) ramen is Yokohama’s own bold, hearty style of ramen — a rich hybrid of creamy tonkotsu (pork-bone) broth and soy-sauce shoyu, topped with thick straight noodles, big sheets of nori, spinach and chashu pork. Born in Yokohama in the 1970s and named for shops ending in “-ya” (家, “house”), it’s famously customisable: you choose your noodle firmness, broth richness and oil level. Filling, savoury and addictive, it’s a Yokohama institution and the perfect counterpoint to the city’s Chinatown.

item.title: Yokohama Oktoberfest Guide: Beer Festival, Tips & Access
item.description: Each autumn, Yokohama’s historic Red Brick Warehouse (Akarenga) on the waterfront transforms into a slice of Bavaria for the city’s hugely popular Oktoberfest — one of Japan’s largest German beer festivals. Beneath the brick facades and harbour lights, long communal tables fill with revellers raising steins of imported German beer, tucking into sausages, pretzels and roast pork while oompah bands play. With its lively atmosphere, bay-side setting and dozens of beers to sample, Yokohama Oktoberfest is a fun, festive evening out — and the same waterfront hosts spring and other seasonal beer events too.

item.title: Yoro Valley Guide: Onsen, Autumn Leaves & Access
item.description: Tucked into the green heart of the Boso Peninsula, Yoro Valley (Yorokeikoku) is Chiba’s premier nature escape — a winding river gorge of clear pools, waterfalls and forested ridges that erupts into brilliant colour each autumn. It’s one of the latest-colouring autumn-leaf spots near Tokyo (late November to early December), and its riverside onsen ryokan let you soak among the foliage. Walking trails lead to the photogenic Awamata Falls and a curious old road tunnel, while the rural Kominato and Isumi railways make getting there half the fun.

item.title: Yosakoi Soran Festival Guide: Dates, Where to Watch & Access
item.description: Every June, Sapporo explodes with colour, music and motion for the Yosakoi Soran Festival — one of Japan’s most exhilarating dance events. Hundreds of teams, tens of thousands of dancers in bold costumes, surge through the streets and across stages, naruko clappers in hand, to powerful remixes of Hokkaido’s traditional “Soran Bushi” fishing song. Born only in 1992, the festival fuses Kochi’s yosakoi dance with Hokkaido’s sea-shanty heritage into a thrilling, modern spectacle that fills Odori Park and the city for several days.

item.title: ZOZO Marine Stadium Guide: Baseball, Bayfront & Access
item.description: Right on Tokyo Bay in the Makuhari Bayfront, ZOZO Marine Stadium is the seaside home of the Chiba Lotte Marines — and one of the most fun, accessible places for visitors to experience a Japanese pro baseball game. Japanese baseball is a spectacle as much as a sport: nonstop organised chanting, team songs, balloon launches and passionate fan sections create an electric, family-friendly atmosphere quite unlike the game in the West.

item.title: Best Hotels & Ryokan in Hiroshima: From Luxury Miyajima to Onomichi U2
item.description: Hiroshima’s accommodation landscape is more varied than the city’s reputation suggests. Central Hiroshima offers reliable international and Japanese business hotels well-positioned for Peace Park and the Shinkansen station. Miyajima island has a handful of historic ryokan with private onsen and views of the Inland Sea — among western Japan’s finest stays. Onomichi’s converted-warehouse Hotel Cycle and the Setoda island’s design-led Azumi Setoda are two of the most stylish small-luxury hotels in Japan.

item.title: Hiroshima Family Trip Guide: Miyajima Deer, Peace Park & Inland Sea Adventures
item.description: Hiroshima is one of the easier Japanese prefectures to visit with children. The headline attractions — Miyajima’s wild deer, the floating torii gate, a samurai castle, a baseball stadium, the Mazda factory tour, the Shimanami Kaido cycling route — work well across age ranges. The compact city centre means short tram rides between sights, and the city’s reputation for friendly, English-tolerant service makes navigation gentler than Tokyo or Kyoto. This guide covers age-appropriate planning, kid-friendly food, and the practical logistics of travelling with children in Hiroshima Prefecture.

item.title: Hiroshima Festivals & Events Guide: Peace Ceremony, Flower Festival & More
item.description: Hiroshima’s festival calendar is unusual in scope. The August 6 Peace Memorial Ceremony is one of the world’s most significant annual commemorations. The Kangensai water music festival on Miyajima is one of Japan’s oldest and most theatrical Shinto rituals. The Flower Festival in early May draws a million visitors. Between them, dozens of smaller neighbourhood matsuri, harvest festivals, and shrine ceremonies fill out the year. This guide is your month-by-month calendar with practical attendance notes for each.

item.title: Hiroshima Girls Trip Guide: Onomichi Cats, Oyster Bars & Miyajima Ryokan
item.description: Hiroshima has the makings of an excellent girls trip — a photogenic floating shrine, a chic ryokan island, hillside temple towns with cat-friendly cafes, lemon-scented spa products from the Setouchi islands, and three days' worth of oyster lunches. The pace is gentler than Tokyo or Osaka, the food is built around small luxuries (fresh oysters, momiji manju, sake tastings), and the photogenic spots are not yet overrun by Instagram tourism. This guide is your three-to-five day Hiroshima girls trip blueprint.

item.title: Hiroshima Goshuin Guide: Itsukushima Shrine, Gokoku Shrine & Temple Seals
item.description: A goshuin (御朱印) is a calligraphic stamp issued by a Shinto shrine or Buddhist temple, hand-written on a folding accordion-style book called a goshuin-cho (御朱印帳). Originally a receipt issued to pilgrims who had copied sutras at a temple, goshuin have become one of the most rewarding souvenirs of a Japan trip — each one is hand-brushed individually, beautifully personal, and impossible to mass-produce. Hiroshima Prefecture is an excellent place to start (or continue) collecting: Itsukushima Shrine issues one of Japan’s most prized goshuin, and the prefecture offers a manageable circuit of major and minor shrines and temples on a single trip.

item.title: Hiroshima Hidden Gems: Onomichi, Tomonoura & the Seto Inland Sea Islands
item.description: Beyond Miyajima and the Peace Park, Hiroshima Prefecture is full of small towns, quiet islands, and obscure corners that most visitors miss entirely. The hillside temple town of Onomichi has been the muse of Japanese filmmakers for a century. Tomonoura’s Edo-era harbour inspired Studio Ghibli. The 18th-century geisha port of Mitarai is barely on the foreign tourist map. The art island of Ikuchijima draws Japanese travellers but few westerners. This guide is for the second or third visit to Hiroshima — or for the first visit if you want the less-trodden version.

item.title: Hiroshima Honeymoon Guide: Miyajima Ryokan, Sunset Seto Views & Setoda Luxury
item.description: A Hiroshima honeymoon trades the obvious Kyoto cherry blossoms for something quieter and more particular. The image that lingers from any honeymoon here is the same one: a vermillion torii standing in calm sea water as the sun sets behind it, the lit corridors of Itsukushima Shrine glowing on stilts beside you. From that core experience, the prefecture offers some of Japan’s most refined luxury ryokan, two of its best small-luxury hotels (Azumi Setoda and Hotel Cycle U2), kayak tours that put you in the shadow of the torii at low light, and a food culture built around the kind of small luxuries — oysters, lemon, sake — that suit a celebration trip.

item.title: Hiroshima Leisure Guide: Shimanami Kaido Cycling, Kayaking & Inland Sea Islands
item.description: Hiroshima has the geography that active travel guides dream of — a chain of bridged islands across a calm inland sea, a sacred mountain rising straight out of the water, kayakable shrine waters, and dozens of small islands each with their own micro-cultures. The leisure landscape here is unusually accessible: rental bikes for the world-famous Shimanami Kaido, half-day kayak tours under the floating torii, and ferry-hopping itineraries that let casual travellers reach quiet islands within an hour of central Hiroshima.

item.title: Hiroshima Mystery & Escape Rooms: Real-Life Puzzle Adventures
item.description: Japan invented the modern “real-life escape game” — known here as Real Escape Game (リアル脱出ゲーム) — and the format has matured into a national pastime with dozens of operators producing increasingly elaborate puzzle experiences. Hiroshima’s scene is smaller than Tokyo’s or Osaka’s but offers a satisfying mix of permanent escape room venues, walking mystery tours, and history-themed puzzle experiences specific to the prefecture. This guide covers what’s actually available for overseas visitors, including English-friendly options.

item.title: Hiroshima Nature Guide: Miyajima, Shimanami Kaido & Taishakukyo Gorge
item.description: Most visitors arrive in Hiroshima expecting a city, and leave surprised by the breadth of its natural landscape. The prefecture stretches from the islands of the Seto Inland Sea up to the mountainous border with Shimane, and along the way passes a sacred forest mountain, two world-class gorges, an island-hopping cycling route considered among the best in Asia, and dozens of small islands with their own micro-cultures of citrus, fishing, and slow time.

item.title: Hiroshima Sightseeing Guide: Peace Memorial, Miyajima & Hiroshima Castle
item.description: Hiroshima is one of those rare cities where the sightseeing list is short, the depth is enormous, and the contrast between sites is dramatic. The Peace Memorial Park and the Atomic Bomb Dome ask you to slow down and confront one of the twentieth century’s most consequential moments. An hour later, a ferry deposits you at Miyajima, where a vermillion torii gate stands in the sea and wild deer wander between thousand-year-old shrine pavilions.

item.title: Hiroshima Solo Travel Guide: Peace Memorial & Shimanami Cycling
item.description: Hiroshima is one of the best Japanese prefectures for solo travel. The headline experiences — Peace Memorial Park, Itsukushima Shrine, Mount Misen, the Shimanami Kaido — are all rewarding to do alone, sometimes more so. The food culture is single-friendly: okonomiyaki counters, ramen bars, izakaya with bar seating, and dozens of conveyor-belt sushi options. The city’s tram network and the JR Ferry to Miyajima are simple enough for solo navigation, and English signage at major sights is reasonably good.

item.title: Comiket Survival Guide: How to Visit Comic Market as an Overseas Fan
item.description: Every year, twice a year, the attention of the anime and manga world swings to a cluster of futuristic buildings on the waterfront of Tokyo Bay. Over three days, more than 700,000 fans pour into Tokyo Big Sight for Comiket — the world’s largest self-published media fair, where over 30,000 independent creator groups (circles) sell their own original comics, art books, games, and music directly to buyers. If Akihabara is anime culture’s permanent home, Comiket is its beating heart.

item.title: Best Hotels & Ryokan in Wakayama
item.description: Wakayama’s accommodation landscape reflects the prefecture’s character precisely: ancient and unusual at the top, practical and unpretentious at the budget end, with a mid-range that favours ryokan and minshuku over business hotels. The most memorable places to sleep in Wakayama cannot be replicated in any other Japanese prefecture — a monastery bedroom at Koyasan where you wake to chanting at dawn, or a Yunomine riverside room where the smell of sulphur mixes with forest air through the open window, are genuinely singular experiences that justify the logistical effort required to reach them.

item.title: Wakayama Events & Festivals: Fire Festivals, Plum Blossom Season & Traditional Celebrations
item.description: Wakayama’s festival calendar is shaped by two things that define the prefecture itself: ancient religious tradition and agricultural cycle. The Kumano Grand Shrines have been hosting ritual ceremonies without interruption for over 1,500 years; the mountain valleys have been marking planting, harvest, and the seasons with community events for as long as anyone can trace. The result is a calendar of genuinely un-performed events — festivals that exist because communities have always done them, not because a tourism board decided a festival would attract visitors.

item.title: Wakayama Family Trip: Pandas, Beach Fun & Kid-Friendly Temples
item.description: Wakayama works well for families in a way that some of Japan’s more densely cultural prefectures do not: there are genuine natural spectacles that children find compelling without requiring adult interpretive scaffolding, a world-class animal park that delivers on its panda promise, beaches that are genuinely safe for small children, and a spiritual mountain that manages to be simultaneously solemn and otherworldly enough to captivate curious kids. The distances between main attractions require planning — this is not a prefecture you can improvise with young children — but a well-structured 3–4 day itinerary produces one of the most varied family travel experiences in western Japan.

item.title: Wakayama Food Guide: Mikan Oranges, Kishu Plums & Kuroshio Seafood
item.description: Wakayama Prefecture’s food identity is inseparable from its geography. The prefecture stretches from the mountains of Koyasan down through deep river valleys to a rugged Pacific coastline swept by the warm Kuroshio Current — one of the ocean’s great fish highways. The warm climate of the Kii Peninsula produces Japan’s finest citrus and most celebrated pickled plums, while the Kuroshio delivers bluefin tuna, spiny lobster, and skipjack caught by fishing fleets that have worked these waters for centuries.

item.title: Wakayama Girls' Trip: Onsen Towns, Cute Cafes & Spiritual Experiences
item.description: Wakayama offers something increasingly rare in Japanese travel: the possibility of genuine experience without the crowds and performance that have come to characterise better-known destinations. A Koyasan calligraphy workshop with a monk as your instructor, attended by a handful of people rather than a tour bus group. A private cave bath in a UNESCO World Heritage spring designed for two. A mikan farm where the farmer’s wife hands you a plastic bag and points at the trees.

item.title: Wakayama Haunted Spots: Ghost Legends of Ancient Pilgrim Routes & Mysterious Forests
item.description: Japan’s ghost traditions — yurei, onryō, kodama, and dozens of more localized supernatural categories — have always been inseparable from the landscape. Mountains, old forests, rivers, and wells are not merely the settings for ghost stories; they are believed in traditional Japanese cosmology to be inhabited by spirits as naturally as they are inhabited by animals. Wakayama Prefecture, with its ancient mountain pilgrimage routes, its UNESCO-listed primeval forests, and its 200,000-grave cemetery that one of Japan’s greatest religious figures is believed to inhabit in living meditation, provides unusually fertile ground for both genuine paranormal tradition and the particular kind of heightened sensory experience that old, dark, and profoundly quiet places reliably produce.

item.title: Wakayama Hidden Gems: Secret Waterfalls, Rural Shrines & Local Fruit Farms
item.description: Most visitors to Wakayama follow the same axis: Koyasan, Shirahama, Nachi Falls. These are the sites that have earned their fame. But Wakayama is a large, mountainous, sparsely populated prefecture — the least densely settled prefecture in Kinki — and the vast majority of it receives essentially no foreign tourism. The river gorges of the interior, the old merchant towns of the coast, the hillside plum orchards that bloom before anyone in Osaka notices, the temple firefly meadows: these places are available to any visitor willing to do a bit of research and not arrive expecting English signage.

item.title: Wakayama Honeymoon: Temple Stays, Secluded Onsen & Coastal Sunsets
item.description: Wakayama offers a honeymoon unlike anything in Europe or Southeast Asia — one shaped by ancient ritual, forested mountains, and a Pacific coastline of genuine drama. The prefecture’s combination of UNESCO pilgrimage trails, mountain temple villages, and Pacific-facing hot spring ryokan means a couple can move from the profound quiet of a Koyasan monastery breakfast to a candlelit room with an ocean-view private bath within a single day’s travel. The romanticism here is slow and earned: it comes from the effort of reaching remote places, from the particular quality of silence in cedar forests at dusk, from the intimacy of sharing a UNESCO-listed stone bath with a single other person.

item.title: Wakayama Leisure: Whale Watching, Adventure World & Plum Picking
item.description: Wakayama is not a prefecture you associate first with leisure in the conventional tourist sense — there are no theme park megaplexes near Osaka here, no manufactured attractions cynically designed for the day-trip market. What Wakayama offers instead is leisure that emerges naturally from the landscape: whale watching from fishing ports where boats have pursued cetaceans for centuries, citrus picking from hillside terraces worked by the same families for generations, paddling through sea caves in warm Kuroshio waters.

item.title: Wakayama Nature: Kumano Kodo Trails, Nachi Falls & Sea Turtle Beaches
item.description: The Kii Peninsula, which makes up most of Wakayama Prefecture, contains some of the most biologically and geologically diverse terrain in Japan. Warm, rain-drenched mountains rise abruptly from a Pacific coastline shaped by the Kuroshio Current — Japan’s equivalent of the Gulf Stream — moderating the climate just enough to support subtropical species more than 300 kilometres north of their usual range. The result is a landscape where ancient cedar forests meet coral reefs, where Japan’s tallest waterfall drops into UNESCO-listed primeval forest, and where sea turtles nest on beaches that also see summer holidaymakers from Osaka.

item.title: Wakayama Onsen Guide: Mountain Hot Springs & Pacific Coast Ryokan
item.description: Wakayama Prefecture contains one of Japan’s highest concentrations of historically significant hot springs — not a coincidence, given that the entire Kii Peninsula sits above the tectonic boundary where the Philippine Sea Plate subducts beneath Honshu, heating groundwater through volcanic activity across a large area. Three of the prefecture’s onsen towns sit directly on the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage network and were healing destinations for emperors, monks, and exhausted pilgrims long before modern tourism existed.

item.title: Wakayama Power Spots: Koyasan Temples, Kumano Shrines & Sacred Mountains
item.description: The concept of power spots (パワースポット, pawā supotto) in Japanese popular spirituality refers to places where spiritual energy — ki, or in the Shinto context, the vitality of enshrined deities — is particularly concentrated and accessible to those who come seeking it.
